summary: Blueprint of Diophantine approximation and transcendence, stages DT.0–DT.5, built on Evertse's Leiden notes (chapters 1–8) and public primary sources, with Mathlib 082e2d3 as the baseline for heights, the product formula, continued fractions, Dirichlet's theorem, Liouville numbers, Mahler measure, Siegel's lemma, Minkowski's theorem, the unit theorem and part of Lindemann–Weierstrass. DT.0 fixes the height conventions (naive height, Mahler measure, Mathlib's absolute Weil height and their comparisons, with the field-extension formula missing at the pin), the house, Siegel's lemma over number fields with rational-integer unknowns, simultaneous Dirichlet approximation and the approximation exponents. DT.1 proves Liouville's inequality with explicit constant, Thue's theorem by the auxiliary-polynomial method and Roth's theorem in full (weighted index, divided derivatives, Wronskians, Roth's lemma, the auxiliary polynomial), with the finiteness of Thue equations. DT.2 states and applies the Subspace Theorem and its p-adic form (Roth from Subspace, Schmidt's approximation by algebraic numbers, norm form equations, Mahler's theorem, S-unit equations in fields of characteristic 0) and decomposes the Evertse–Ferretti proof to the level of its numbered results. DT.3 proves Hermite, Lindemann–Weierstrass in Baker's form, Gelfond–Schneider (real case by Evertse's route, complex case by Gelfond's method) and Baker's linear independence of logarithms by the Schneider–Lang method of Waldschmidt, and states Baker's, Matveev's and Yu's quantitative bounds exactly. DT.4 derives effective finiteness for unit, Thue, superelliptic, Catalan-type and S-unit equations from those bounds, with the height, degree and branch conversion lemmas, and exports the bound theorems to EffectiveDiophantineMethods ED.2. DT.5 defines Mahler functions, E- and G-functions and states Siegel–Shidlovskii (Beukers' refinement), André, Nishioka, Nesterenko, Ax–Schanuel and Schanuel's and the period conjectures as explicit hypotheses. Open: the proofs of the quantitative linear-form bounds, the imported inputs of the Subspace Theorem's proof, several DT.4 and DT.5 proofs without public sources, part of the absolute-height API, and the requests to GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic and ClassicalArithmeticCompletion.

nodes.title: The primitive minimal polynomial F_x ∈ ℤ[X] of an algebraic number
nodes.statement: Let F be a field of characteristic zero and x ∈ F. If x is algebraic over ℚ, its primitive minimal polynomial F_x ∈ ℤ[X] is the unique polynomial with integer coefficients that (a) is primitive (the gcd of its coefficients is 1), (b) has positive leading coefficient a₀ > 0, and (c) is a rational multiple of the minimal polynomial minpoly ℚ x. Equivalently F_x = a₀·minpoly ℚ x with a₀ the least common multiple of the denominators of the coefficients of minpoly ℚ x, and F_x = a₀ ∏_{i=1}^{d} (X − x^{(i)}) over ℂ, where d = deg x and x^{(1)}, …, x^{(d)} are the complex conjugates of x. Construction: clear the denominators of minpoly ℚ x (Mathlib's integer normalization), take the primitive part, and change the sign if the leading coefficient is negative. Convention (pinned): F_x := 1 when x is transcendental over ℚ.
hypotheses: F is any field of characteristic zero; the definition carries no algebraicity hypothesis and returns the junk value 1 for transcendental x.
The sign is fixed by a₀ > 0; without it F_x is determined only up to ±1.

The junk value 1 is chosen so that the naive height, the Mahler measure and Mathlib's absolute height (whose junk value is 1) all equal 1 at transcendental x, which keeps the comparison theorems free of algebraicity hypotheses.
proofSteps: Let m = minpoly ℚ x; for algebraic x it is monic and irreducible (minpoly.irreducible).

IsLocalization.integerNormalization clears the denominators of m and keeps its roots (IsLocalization.integerNormalization_aeval_eq_zero); its primitive part is primitive (Polynomial.isPrimitive_primPart); multiply by −1 if the leading coefficient is negative.

Characterisation: a primitive P ∈ ℤ[X] with positive leading coefficient, irreducible and vanishing at x, equals F_x. Both are ℚ-multiples of m (minpoly.dvd and irreducibility), and two ℚ-proportional primitive integer polynomials with positive leading coefficients are equal (Polynomial.IsPrimitive.Int.dvd_iff_map_cast_dvd_map_cast applied in both directions).
Divisibility: every P ∈ ℤ[X] with P(x) = 0 is divisible by F_x in ℤ[X]: m ∣ P in ℚ[X] (minpoly.dvd), hence F_x ∣ P in ℚ[X], hence in ℤ[X] by Gauss's lemma since F_x is primitive.
Irreducibility in ℤ[X] follows from irreducibility of m in ℚ[X] and primitivity (Polynomial.IsPrimitive.Int.irreducible_iff_irreducible_map_cast).
Lemma 3.7 of Evertse (a₀·x is an algebraic integer) is Mathlib's isIntegral_leadingCoeff_smul applied to F_x; hence den(x) ∣ a₀ (Algebra.natDenominator_dvd_iff).
acceptance: F_{2/3} = 3X − 2 and, for x = (1 + 2√3)/5, F_x = 25X² − 10X − 11 (Evertse's example, p. 41).
For an algebraic integer x, F_x = minpoly ℤ x; for x = 1/2 it differs from minpoly ℤ (1/2), which is 0 because 1/2 is not integral.
deg F_x = deg minpoly ℚ x for every x (both 0 at transcendental x).

nodes.title: The naive height H(x) of an algebraic number
nodes.statement: For x in a field of characteristic zero, the naive height is H(x) := max_i |a_i|, the maximum of the absolute values of the coefficients a_0, …, a_d of the primitive minimal polynomial F_x = a_0 X^d + ⋯ + a_d; as a declaration it is Mathlib's sup norm of F_x (Polynomial.supNorm), valued in ℝ. For a rational x/y in lowest terms, H(x/y) = max(|x|, |y|) (see DT.0/naive-height-of-rational). Convention (pinned): H(x) = 1 for transcendental x (F_x = 1).
hypotheses: No algebraicity hypothesis in the definition; transcendental x gets 1.
H is the height of the polynomial F_x, not the absolute Weil height: H(√2) = 2 while Mathlib's absMulHeight₁ √2 = √2.
proofSteps: Define H(x) := supNorm(F_x); supNorm_def' identifies it with the maximum of |a_i|.
H(x) ≥ 1 because F_x is a nonzero integer polynomial.
Invariance under field embeddings and conjugation is inherited from primitiveMinpoly_map and primitiveMinpoly_eq_of_minpoly_eq.
H(x⁻¹) = H(x): F_{x⁻¹} is the reversed polynomial X^d F_x(1/X), up to sign (Evertse Exercise 3.1(i)); for x = 0 both sides are H(0) = 1.

(H(x) + 1)⁻¹ ≤ |x| ≤ H(x) + 1 for nonzero algebraic x ∈ ℂ: the upper bound is Cauchy's bound (Polynomial.IsRoot.norm_lt_cauchyBound with |a_0| ≥ 1), the lower bound is the upper bound applied to x⁻¹ (Evertse Exercise 3.1(ii)).
den(x) ≤ a_0 ≤ H(x) from natDenominator_dvd_leadingCoeff_primitiveMinpoly.
acceptance: H(0) = 1 since F_0 = X.
The two conventions are distinguished: H(√2) = 2, absMulHeight₁ √2 = √2; they agree on ℚ (DT.0/naive-height-of-rational).

nodes.title: The Mahler measure M(x) of an algebraic number
nodes.statement: For x in a field of characteristic zero, M(x) := M(F_x), Mathlib's Mahler measure of the primitive minimal polynomial F_x mapped to ℂ[X] (Polynomial.mapMahlerMeasure along ℤ → ℂ). By Jensen's formula M(x) = a₀ ∏_{i=1}^{d} max(1, |x^{(i)}|), where a₀ > 0 is the leading coefficient of F_x and x^{(1)}, …, x^{(d)} are the complex conjugates of x (the roots of minpoly ℚ x in ℂ). Convention (pinned): M(x) = 1 for transcendental x.
hypotheses: No algebraicity hypothesis; M(x) = M(1) = 1 at transcendental x.
The leading coefficient a₀ is part of M(x): M(1/2) = 2, not 1/2.
proofSteps: Define M(x) := (F_x.map (ℤ → ℂ)).mahlerMeasure.

Jensen's formula for complex polynomials (Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_eq_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_roots) and the equality of the complex roots of F_x with those of minpoly ℚ x (map_primitiveMinpoly) give the product formula API item.
M(x) ≥ a₀ ≥ 1 since all factors max(1, |x^{(i)}|) are ≥ 1.

nodes.title: The house ⌈x⌉ of an algebraic number, independent of the number field
nodes.statement: For x in a field of characteristic zero, the house is ⌈x⌉ := max{|z| : z ∈ ℂ a root of minpoly ℚ x}, the largest absolute value of a complex conjugate of x. For x in a number field K it equals Mathlib's NumberField.house x = max_{σ : K → ℂ} |σ(x)| (Evertse (3.2)). Convention (pinned): ⌈x⌉ = 0 for transcendental x (empty set of roots).
hypotheses: x in any characteristic-zero field; the conjugates are taken in ℂ through minpoly ℚ x, so no embedding into ℂ is chosen.
proofSteps: Define ⌈x⌉ := ⨆_{z ∈ rootSet (minpoly ℚ x) ℂ} |z| (a supremum over a finite set; 0 over the empty set).

Compatibility with Mathlib: for x ∈ K, the images σ(x), σ : K → ℂ, are exactly the roots of minpoly ℚ x (NumberField.Embeddings.range_eval_eq_rootSet_minpoly), so the two maxima coincide (NumberField.house_eq_sup').

Submultiplicativity, subadditivity and ⌈x^n⌉ = ⌈x⌉^n (Evertse Exercise 3.5): compute in K = ℚ(x, y) via the compatibility and Mathlib's NumberField.house_mul_le, house_add_le; for powers, the conjugates of x^n are the n-th powers of conjugates of x, each attained by an embedding of ℚ(x).
1 ≤ ⌈x⌉ for nonzero algebraic integers (Evertse Lemma 3.6 = NumberField.exists_conjugate_one_le_norm).
⌈x⌉ = 1 iff x is a root of unity, for nonzero algebraic integers (Evertse Exercise 3.6(iv); NumberField.Embeddings.pow_eq_one_of_norm_eq_one in K = ℚ(x) with Lemma 3.6).
For algebraic integers ⌈x⌉ ≤ M(x) (every factor of M(x) = ∏ max(1,|x^{(i)}|) is ≥ 1 and one of them is ⌈x⌉ or 1), and in general M(x) ≤ a₀ max(1, ⌈x⌉)^d (Smyth (6)).
acceptance: For x ∈ K a number field, house x = NumberField.house x, independently of K.

nodes.title: The irrationality exponent μ(ξ) ∈ [1, ∞]
nodes.statement: For ξ ∈ ℝ, the irrationality exponent is μ(ξ) := sup { p ∈ ℝ : LiouvilleWith p ξ } ∈ [1, ∞], taken in ℝ≥0∞ (the supremum of ENNReal.ofReal p over the p with LiouvilleWith p ξ), where Mathlib's LiouvilleWith p ξ means: there is C with |ξ − m/n| < C/n^p and ξ ≠ m/n for infinitely many n ∈ ℕ (with some m ∈ ℤ). Pinned values: μ(ξ) = 1 for every rational ξ, μ(ξ) ≥ 2 for every irrational ξ, and μ(ξ) = ∞ exactly for Liouville numbers. For irrational ξ, μ(ξ) = sup{p : |ξ − r| < den(r)^{-p} for infinitely many r ∈ ℚ}, the exponent of Sondow's Definition 2 and of Bugeaud (μ = w₁ + 1).
hypotheses: ξ ∈ ℝ arbitrary; rationals get the value 1 rather than being excluded.
The condition ξ ≠ m/n in LiouvilleWith is essential: without it every rational number would get exponent ∞.
Values in ℝ≥0∞ so that Liouville numbers get ⊤; the set of admissible p is downward closed (LiouvilleWith.mono) and contains 1 (liouvilleWith_one).
proofSteps: Define μ(ξ) := ⨆_{p} ⨆_{LiouvilleWith p ξ} ofReal p.
1 ≤ μ(ξ) by liouvilleWith_one; LiouvilleWith p ξ for every real p with ofReal p < μ(ξ) by LiouvilleWith.mono.
μ(ξ) = ⊤ ↔ Liouville ξ by forall_liouvilleWith_iff.
Rational ξ = a/b: |ξ − m/n| ≥ 1/(bn) when nonzero, so LiouvilleWith p fails for p > 1; hence μ = 1.
Irrational ξ: Real.infinite_rat_abs_sub_lt_one_div_den_sq_of_irrational gives LiouvilleWith 2, so μ ≥ 2; conversely μ ≥ 2 > 1 gives LiouvilleWith p for some p > 1 and LiouvilleWith.irrational.
Invariance under ξ ↦ ξ + r, rξ (r ∈ ℚ^×), −ξ from the LiouvilleWith add_rat_iff, mul_rat_iff, neg_iff lemmas.
Almost every ξ has μ(ξ) = 2: ae_not_liouvilleWith (no LiouvilleWith p with p > 2 almost everywhere) and irrationality almost everywhere.
Rational-approximation form for irrational ξ: a solution m/n of LiouvilleWith gives the reduced fraction r = m/n with den(r) ≤ n, and conversely; the constant C is absorbed by any smaller exponent.
acceptance: μ(1/2) = 1, μ(√2) = 2 (Dirichlet and Mathlib's Liouville inequality Liouville.exists_pos_real_of_irrational_root with degree 2), μ(liouvilleNumber 10) = ⊤.
μ(0) ≠ ⊤, which a definition forgetting ξ ≠ m/n would violate.
Roth's theorem (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.1/roth-theorem) is the statement μ(α) = 2 for real algebraic irrational α; Liouville's inequality gives μ(α) ≤ deg α.

sources.excerpt: If α has irrationality measure f(x, µ) = x^{−µ} for some µ = µ(α), then µ(α) ∈ [2, ∞) is called the irrationality exponent of α. If there is no such µ, then we write µ(α) = ∞ and we call α a Liouville number.

nodes.title: The exponent w(θ) of approximation to zero by the linear form x₀ + x₁θ₁ + ⋯ + xₙθₙ
nodes.statement: For θ = (θ₁, …, θₙ) ∈ ℝⁿ, w(θ) ∈ ℝ≥0∞ is the supremum of the real w for which 0 < |x₀ + x₁θ₁ + ⋯ + xₙθₙ| ≤ ‖x‖^{-w} holds for infinitely many x = (x₀, …, xₙ) ∈ ℤ^{n+1}, where ‖x‖ = max_j |x_j| (supremum of ofReal w, so negative w contribute 0). Mahler's exponent is w_n(ξ) := w(ξ, ξ², …, ξⁿ): the supremum of w with 0 < |P(ξ)| ≤ H(P)^{-w} for infinitely many P ∈ ℤ[X] of degree ≤ n (Bugeaud, Definition 2.1).
hypotheses: θ ∈ ℝⁿ, n ≥ 0; for n = 0 the form is x₀ and w = 0.
The condition 0 < |…| excludes exact vanishing; without it a rational θ would get exponent ∞.
The height of x is the maximum norm of the full vector (x₀, …, xₙ), as in Bugeaud's H(P).
proofSteps: Define w(θ) := ⨆_{w} ⨆_{the solution set is infinite} ofReal w, with θ extended by θ₀ = 1 (Fin.cons 1 θ).
The admissible set of w is downward closed, so w(θ) ≥ ofReal w as soon as the set for w is infinite (API item le_linearFormExponent_of_infinite).

For n = 1 and irrational ξ: 0 < |x₀ + x₁ξ| ≤ ‖x‖^{-w} with x₁ ≠ 0 is equivalent, up to constants absorbed in the exponent, to |ξ + x₀/x₁| ≤ |x₁|^{-1-w}, so w(ξ) + 1 = μ(ξ) (API item linearFormExponent_one_add, using ‖x‖ ≍ |x₁| for good approximations).
Monotonicity of Mahler's exponent in n: the polynomials of degree ≤ m are among those of degree ≤ n.
acceptance: w(√2) = 1 and w(1/2) = 0 (for rational θ the nonzero values are ≥ 1/den, so only w ≤ 0 has infinitely many solutions).
DT.0/linear-form-exponent-dirichlet-bound gives w(θ) ≥ n when 1, θ₁, …, θₙ are ℚ-linearly independent.

nodes.title: The exponent λ(θ) of simultaneous rational approximation
nodes.statement: For θ = (θ₁, …, θₙ) ∈ ℝⁿ, λ(θ) ∈ ℝ≥0∞ is the supremum of the real λ for which max_j |x₀θ_j − x_j| ≤ |x₀|^{-λ} holds for infinitely many (x₀, x₁, …, xₙ) ∈ ℤ^{n+1} with x₀ ≠ 0. The exponent of Bugeaud's Definition 2.2 is λ_n(ξ) = λ(ξ, ξ², …, ξⁿ).
hypotheses: θ ∈ ℝⁿ, n ≥ 0; for n = 0 the condition is vacuous and λ = ∞.
If all θ_j are rational, λ(θ) = ∞ (multiples of a common denominator give exact solutions); the exponent is informative when some θ_j is irrational.
proofSteps: Define λ(θ) := ⨆_{λ} ⨆_{the solution set is infinite} ofReal λ.
For n = 1 and irrational ξ: |x₀ξ − x₁| ≤ |x₀|^{-λ} is |ξ − x₁/x₀| ≤ |x₀|^{-1-λ}, so λ(ξ) + 1 = μ(ξ).
Dropping coordinates can only enlarge the solution sets, so λ(θ) ≤ λ(θ ∘ f) for injective f.
All θ_j rational: with D a common denominator, (kD, kDθ) are exact solutions for all k.

nodes.statement: For n ∈ ℕ and ξ ∈ ℝ, w*_n(ξ) ∈ ℝ≥0∞ is the supremum of the real w for which 0 < |ξ − α| ≤ H(α)^{-w-1} holds for infinitely many algebraic α ∈ ℂ of degree at most n, where H is the naive height (DT.0/naive-height-of-algebraic-number). hypotheses: The −1 in the exponent makes w*_1 = w₁ = μ − 1 on irrationals.

nodes.title: Badly approximable real numbers
nodes.statement: A real number ξ is badly approximable if ξ is irrational and there is c > 0 with q · ‖qξ‖ ≥ c for every integer q ≥ 1, where ‖t‖ = |t − round t| is the distance to the nearest integer.
hypotheses: Irrationality is part of the definition, as in the source; rationals are never badly approximable.
proofSteps: Define BadlyApproximable ξ := Irrational ξ ∧ ∃ c > 0, ∀ q ≥ 1, c ≤ q·|qξ − round(qξ)|.
Badly approximable ⇒ μ(ξ) = 2: |ξ − m/n| ≥ c/n² excludes LiouvilleWith p for p > 2, and irrationality gives μ ≥ 2.

Quadratic irrationals are badly approximable: Mathlib's Liouville inequality Liouville.exists_pos_real_of_irrational_root applied to the degree-2 minimal polynomial gives |ξ − a/b| ≥ c/b² (Evertse Exercise 2.7 for √d).
Badly approximable numbers are not Liouville numbers (μ = 2 < ⊤).
Invariance under ξ ↦ ξ + r and ξ ↦ rξ for r ∈ ℚ^× by rescaling c with the denominator of r.
acceptance: √2 and the golden ratio are badly approximable; no rational number and no Liouville number is.

nodes.title: Littlewood's conjecture, as a statement
nodes.statement: Littlewood's conjecture is the proposition: for all α, β ∈ ℝ and every ε > 0 there is an integer y ≥ 1 with y · ‖yα‖ · ‖yβ‖ < ε, where ‖t‖ is the distance from t to the nearest integer. It is recorded as a statement (a proposition to be used as an explicit hypothesis), not as a theorem; this stage proves the cases it reduces to and the Dirichlet bound y‖yα‖‖yβ‖ ≤ 1 for infinitely many y.
hypotheses: The conjecture is open; no consumer may use it except as an explicit hypothesis.
It reduces to pairs (α, β) of badly approximable numbers: if α is rational or not badly approximable, the inequality holds with ‖yβ‖ ≤ 1/2.
proofSteps: Define LittlewoodConjecture : Prop := ∀ α β, ∀ ε > 0, ∃ y ≥ 1, y‖yα‖‖yβ‖ < ε.
If α is not badly approximable (in particular rational or Liouville), then inf_y y‖yα‖ = 0 and ‖yβ‖ ≤ 1/2 give the inequality.

Infinitely many y with y‖yα‖‖yβ‖ ≤ 1: if α, β are not both rational apply the simultaneous Dirichlet theorem with n = 2 (‖yα‖, ‖yβ‖ ≤ y^{-1/2}); if both are rational take multiples of a common denominator (Evertse p. 22).
acceptance: The statement holds for α rational and for α = liouvilleNumber 10; the one-dimensional analogue (∀ α, inf_y y‖yα‖ = 0) is false, witness √2.

sources.excerpt: Littlewood’s Conjecture. Let α1, α2 be any two real numbers. Then for every ε > 0 there exists a positive integer y such that y∥α1y∥ · ∥α2y∥ < ε.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

sources.excerpt: This implies that there are inﬁnitely many positive integers y such that y∥α1y∥ · ∥α2y∥ ⩽ 1. In fact, this is true also if both α1, α2 ∈ Q,

nodes.title: The naive height of a rational number: H(x/y) = max(|x|, |y|) = Mathlib's height
nodes.statement: For q ∈ ℚ with q = x/y in lowest terms (y = den q > 0, x = num q), and for q viewed in any field F of characteristic zero, H(q) = max(|x|, y) and H(q) = Height.mulHeight₁ q, the multiplicative height of q ∈ ℚ in Mathlib's normalisation.
hypotheses: x, y coprime with y > 0; the value does not depend on the field F in which q is viewed.
proofSteps: F_q = yX − x (API item primitiveMinpoly_ratCast): it is primitive since gcd(x, y) = 1, has positive leading coefficient y, and vanishes at q.
Hence H(q) = supNorm(yX − x) = max(|x|, y).
Mathlib's Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max gives mulHeight₁ q = max(|num q|, den q).
acceptance: H(2/3) = 3, H(−5/2) = 5, H(0) = 1 = mulHeight₁ 0, H(n) = max(|n|, 1) for n ∈ ℤ.
This is the height H(ξ) of Evertse's Chapter 6 used in Liouville's and Roth's theorems (DT.1).

sources.excerpt: Let α = a/b with a, b ∈ Z, b > 0, gcd(a, b) = 1. Then α has primitive minimal polynomial bX − a, hence H(α) = max(|a|, b).
sources.match: Exactly the first equality.

sources.excerpt: Recall that the height H(ξ) of a rational number ξ is given by H(ξ) := max(|x|, |y|), where x, y are coprime integers such that ξ = x/y.
sources.match: The convention consumed by Chapter 6 (DT.1).

nodes.title: The house computed in any number field: ⌈x⌉ = NumberField.house x
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and x ∈ K. Then the field-independent house ⌈x⌉ = max{|z| : z ∈ ℂ, minpoly ℚ x (z) = 0} equals Mathlib's NumberField.house x = max_{σ : K → ℂ} |σ(x)|.
hypotheses: K any number field containing x; the right-hand side depends on K only through x.
proofSteps: The set {σ(x) : σ : K →+* ℂ} equals the set of complex roots of minpoly ℚ x (NumberField.Embeddings.range_eval_eq_rootSet_minpoly).
NumberField.house_eq_sup' writes NumberField.house x as the maximum of |σ(x)| over the embeddings; both maxima are over the same finite nonempty set.
acceptance: For K = ℚ(√2) and x = 1 + √2: both sides are 1 + √2.

sources.excerpt: ⌈α⌉ = max(|σ1(α)|, . . . , |σd(α)|) for α ∈ K, for by Corollary 3.13, the sequence σ1(α), . . . , σd(α) consists of the conjugates of α, each repeated exactly [K : Q(α)] = d/m times.
sources.match: Exactly the statement; the set form of Corollary 3.13 suffices for a maximum.

nodes.title: F_x is a₀ times the minimal polynomial; its complex roots are the conjugates
nodes.statement: Let x be algebraic over ℚ in a field of characteristic zero, with primitive minimal polynomial F_x of leading coefficient a₀. Then the image of F_x in ℚ[X] is a₀·minpoly ℚ x; consequently deg F_x = deg x, and the multiset of complex roots of F_x is the multiset of complex roots of minpoly ℚ x (the d distinct conjugates x^{(1)}, …, x^{(d)}), so F_x = a₀ ∏_{i=1}^{d} (X − x^{(i)}) in ℂ[X]. The same holds in any field L over which minpoly ℚ x splits.
hypotheses: x algebraic over ℚ; the roots are distinct because minpoly ℚ x is separable in characteristic zero.
proofSteps: By construction F_x is a ℚ-multiple c·minpoly ℚ x (integer normalization and primitive part); comparing leading coefficients, c = a₀ since minpoly ℚ x is monic.
A field L in which minpoly ℚ x splits (ℂ, or a splitting field) gives minpoly ℚ x = ∏ (X − r) over its roots (Polynomial.C_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_multiset_X_sub_C), hence F_x = a₀ ∏ (X − r).

nodes.title: Regrouping a product over the infinite places of L by the places of K below
nodes.statement: Let K ⊆ L be number fields (an algebra K → L) and g : InfinitePlace K → M a map to a commutative monoid. Then ∏_{w ∈ InfinitePlace L} g(w|_K)^{mult w} = ∏_{v ∈ InfinitePlace K} g(v)^{mult v · [L:K]}, where w|_K = w.comap (algebraMap K L). Equivalently, for every infinite place v of K, ∑_{w | v} mult w = mult v · [L:K].
hypotheses: mult w ∈ {1, 2} is 1 at real and 2 at complex places, as in Mathlib's product formula.
proofSteps: Group the factors over w by v = w|_K (a finite partition of InfinitePlace L).
For w over v, mult w = mult v · [L_w : K_v] (NumberField.InfinitePlace.mult_mul_finrank), and [L_w : K_v] is the inertia degree of w over v (NumberField.InfinitePlace.inertiaDeg_eq_finrank).
∑_{w | v} inertiaDeg = [L:K] (NumberField.InfinitePlace.sum_inertiaDeg_eq_finrank), hence ∑_{w|v} mult w = mult v · [L:K] and the product regroups as stated.
acceptance: K = ℚ, L = ℚ(i): the one complex place of L has mult 2 = 1·[L:ℚ].
K = ℚ, L = ℚ(√2): two real places, each of mult 1, total 2.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 2.2. Let x ∈ K \ {0} and y ∈ L \ {0}. Then ∑_{w|v} log |x|w = log |x|v
sources.match: The same identity for normalised absolute values, whose normalisation carries the local degrees (our mult w and inertia degrees).

nodes.title: Heights under finite extension: H_L(x) = H_K(x)^{[L:K]}
nodes.statement: Let K ⊆ L be number fields, ι a finite type and x : ι → K. Then Height.mulHeight (algebraMap K L ∘ x) = Height.mulHeight x ^ [L:K], where each side is Mathlib's relative multiplicative height in its own field (NumberField.instAdmissibleAbsValues). Applied to ![x, 1] (Height.mulHeight₁_eq_mulHeight) it gives mulHeight₁ of x computed in L = (mulHeight₁ of x computed in K)^{[L:K]}.
hypotheses: Mathlib's number-field heights are relative (not normalised by the degree); this is the formula that makes (mulHeight₁)^{1/[K:ℚ]} independent of K.
For the zero tuple both sides are 1 (junk value).
proofSteps: If x = 0 both sides are 1. Otherwise write both heights by NumberField.mulHeight_eq as (∏_{infinite} (sup_i |x_i|_v)^{mult v})·∏ᶠ_{finite} sup_i |x_i|_v.
Infinite part: w(algebraMap y) = (w|_K)(y) (NumberField.InfinitePlace.comap_apply); apply DT.0/infinite-places-over with g(v) = sup_i v(x_i).

Finite part: every finite place of L is given by a maximal ideal P of 𝓞 L lying over a unique maximal ideal p of 𝓞 K, and P(algebraMap y) = p(y)^{e(P|p) f(P|p)} (NumberField.FinitePlace.equivHeightOneSpectrum_symm_apply_algebraMap); the power commutes with the supremum over i.

Group the finite product by p (only finitely many factors differ from 1 because x ≠ 0) and use ∑_{P|p} e(P|p) f(P|p) = rank_{𝓞K} 𝓞L = [L:K] (Ideal.sum_ramification_inertia_eq_finrank; 𝓞L is finite flat over 𝓞K, and its rank is [L:K] by comparing NumberField.RingOfIntegers.rank for K and L with the tower law Module.finrank_mul_finrank).
Multiply the two parts.
acceptance: K = ℚ, L = ℚ(i), x = 1/2: mulHeight₁ in ℚ is 2, in ℚ(i) it is 4 = 2².
Consequently NumberField.absMulHeight₁ is independent of the field (DT.0/abs-mul-height-eq-rpow).

sources.excerpt: Proof. Let L be another number ﬁeld containing the coordinates x0, · · · , xn of x. We can assume that K ⊂ L. Then ∑_{w∈MK} max_j log |xj|w = ∑_{v∈MK} ∑_{w|v} max_j log |xj|w

nodes.title: Heights are invariant under isomorphisms of number fields
nodes.statement: Let e : K ≃+* K' be an isomorphism of number fields, ι finite and x : ι → K. Then Height.mulHeight (e ∘ x) = Height.mulHeight x; in particular mulHeight₁ (e x) = mulHeight₁ x.
hypotheses: e is any ring isomorphism (automatically ℚ-linear).
proofSteps: Make K' a K-algebra through e; then algebraMap K K' = e and [K':K] = 1 because e is a K-linear bijection.
Apply DT.0/mul-height-algebra-map: the exponent is 1.
acceptance: Complex conjugation on ℚ(i) preserves heights: mulHeight₁(2 + i) = mulHeight₁(2 − i).

sources.excerpt: Thus H : Q →R. Note that all algebraic closures of Q are isomorphic.
sources.match: The isomorphism invariance used to make H well defined on Q̄.

nodes.title: Mathlib's absolute height computed in any number field
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and x ∈ K. Then NumberField.absMulHeight₁ x = (mulHeight₁ x)^{1/[K:ℚ]}, the multiplicative height of x computed in K raised to 1/[K:ℚ].
hypotheses: Mathlib defines absMulHeight₁ through the subfield ℚ⟮x⟯; this lemma removes the dependence on that choice.
proofSteps: By definition absMulHeight₁ x = (mulHeight₁ of the generator of ℚ⟮x⟯)^{1/[ℚ⟮x⟯:ℚ]} (x is integral over ℚ).
DT.0/mul-height-algebra-map for ℚ⟮x⟯ ⊆ K (the inclusion sends the generator to x) gives mulHeight₁ x = (mulHeight₁ gen)^{[K:ℚ⟮x⟯]}.
The tower law [K:ℚ] = [K:ℚ⟮x⟯]·[ℚ⟮x⟯:ℚ] (Module.finrank_mul_finrank) and positivity of heights give the claim.
acceptance: x = 2 ∈ ℚ(i): mulHeight₁ in ℚ(i) is 4, so absMulHeight₁ 2 = 4^{1/2} = 2.

sources.excerpt: Deﬁnition 2.7. Weil Height Let P ∈ K∗ be a point, then H(P) = HK(P)^{1/[K:Q]}. Again, the above result shows that the deﬁnition of the height is independent of choice of K.
sources.match: Exactly the statement.

sources.excerpt: h(α) := log M/d = ∑_{all ν} log+ |α|ν^{dν/d}. (5) Here h(α) is called the Weil, or absolute height of α.
sources.match: The same normalisation.

nodes.title: The absolute height depends only on the minimal polynomial
nodes.statement: Let F, F' be fields of characteristic zero and x ∈ F, y ∈ F' with minpoly ℚ x = minpoly ℚ y. Then NumberField.absMulHeight₁ x = NumberField.absMulHeight₁ y. In particular conjugate algebraic numbers have equal absolute height, and absMulHeight₁(φ x) = absMulHeight₁ x for every ring homomorphism φ : F → F'.
hypotheses: If x, y are transcendental both sides are Mathlib's junk value 1.
proofSteps: Transcendental case: both minimal polynomials are 0 and both heights are 1.

Algebraic case: IntermediateField.adjoinRootEquivAdjoin gives ℚ-algebra isomorphisms AdjoinRoot m ≅ ℚ⟮x⟯ and AdjoinRoot m ≅ ℚ⟮y⟯ (m the common minimal polynomial) sending the root to the generators; compose to ℚ⟮x⟯ ≅ ℚ⟮y⟯ with gen x ↦ gen y.
DT.0/mul-height-ring-equiv gives equal mulHeight₁ of the generators, and the degrees agree (IntermediateField.adjoin.finrank); so the absolute heights agree.
acceptance: absMulHeight₁ √2 = absMulHeight₁ (−√2) = √2.
For φ : ℚ(i) → ℂ, absMulHeight₁(φ(1 + i)) = absMulHeight₁(1 + i) = √2.

sources.excerpt: Thus H : Q →R. Note that all algebraic closures of Q are isomorphic.
sources.match: Well-definedness of H on Q̄, which is the invariance under isomorphisms of subfields.
The right-hand side depends only on the conjugates of α, i.e. on its minimal polynomial.

nodes.title: A primitive integer polynomial has Gauss norm 1 at every finite place of a number field
nodes.statement: Let L be a number field, w a finite place of L and P ∈ ℤ[X] primitive. Then the Gauss norm of P mapped to L[X] at w (with radius 1), max_i w(a_i) over the coefficients a_i of P, equals 1.
hypotheses: P primitive, in particular P ≠ 0.
proofSteps: Every coefficient is a rational integer, and w(n) ≤ 1 for n ∈ ℤ (NumberField.HeightOneSpectrum.adicAbv_intCast_le_one), so the Gauss norm is ≤ 1.
Primitive over ℤ means the gcd of the coefficients is 1; by Bezout (Finset.gcd_eq_sum_mul) 1 = ∑ a_i u_i with u_i ∈ ℤ.
By the ultrametric inequality (NumberField.FinitePlace.add_le) 1 = w(1) ≤ max_i w(a_i) w(u_i) ≤ max_i w(a_i). (Mathlib's Rat.iSup_finitePlace_apply_eq_one_of_gcd_eq_one is the same argument over ℚ.)
acceptance: P = 2X − 1 at a place above 2 of ℚ(√2): coefficients have w-values w(2) < 1 and w(1) = 1, Gauss norm 1.

sources.excerpt: coming from the product formula, and from considering the Newton polygons of the irreducible factors (of degree dν) of Pα over Qp
sources.match: Smyth's route to |a₀| = ∏_p ∏_{ν|p} max(1, |α|_ν^{dν}); ours replaces Newton polygons by Gauss norms, of which this lemma is the primitivity input.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.1. If v is not archimedean, then |fg|v = |f|v|g|v.
sources.match: Gauss's lemma in the Gauss-norm form; a primitive integer polynomial has |f|_v = 1.

nodes.title: Gauss's lemma at a finite place: |a₀|_w ∏ max(1, |αᵢ|_w) = 1
nodes.statement: Let L be a number field, w a finite place of L, P ∈ ℤ[X] primitive, and suppose P = a·∏_{b ∈ s} (X − b) in L[X] for some a ∈ L and a multiset s of elements of L. Then w(a) · ∏_{b ∈ s} max(w(b), 1) = 1.
hypotheses: P splits over L with leading coefficient a (the image of the leading coefficient of P).
proofSteps: w is nonarchimedean (NumberField.FinitePlace.add_le), so the Gauss norm at w with radius 1 is multiplicative (Polynomial.gaussNorm_mul).
The Gauss norm of C a is w(a) (Polynomial.gaussNorm_C); the Gauss norm of X − C b is max(w(b), 1), from its two coefficients −b and 1.
Hence w(a) ∏ max(w(b), 1) is the Gauss norm of P, which is 1 by DT.0/gauss-norm-primitive-finite-place.
acceptance: P = 2X − 1 = 2(X − 1/2) over ℚ at the 2-adic place: |2|₂ · max(|1/2|₂, 1) = (1/2)·2 = 1.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.1. If v is not archimedean, then |fg|v = |f|v|g|v. Proof. The inequality |fg|v ≤ |f|v|g|v is immediate because v is not archimedean.
sources.match: The multiplicativity used; the lemma is its application to the factorisation of P.

nodes.title: Mahler measure and absolute height: M(x) = H_abs(x)^{deg x}
nodes.statement: For every x in a field of characteristic zero, M(x) = absMulHeight₁(x)^{d} with d = deg minpoly ℚ x, where M is DT.0/mahler-measure-of-algebraic-number and absMulHeight₁ is Mathlib's absolute multiplicative height. Equivalently log M(x) = d · h(x) with h the absolute logarithmic Weil height. For transcendental x both sides are 1.
hypotheses: No algebraicity hypothesis: transcendental x gives 1 = 1^0 with the pinned junk values.
The multiplicities of Mathlib's product formula (mult w = 2 at complex places) are exactly those that make the archimedean part equal to ∏ over all complex embeddings.
proofSteps: Transcendental x: M(x) = M(1) = 1 and absMulHeight₁ x = 1, d = 0.

Algebraic x of degree d: let L be the splitting field of minpoly ℚ x (Polynomial.SplittingField; a number field) and β₁, …, β_d ∈ L the roots, so F_x = a₀ ∏ (X − β_i) in L[X] (DT.0/map-primitive-minpoly, Polynomial.SplittingField.splits).
Finite places: for every finite place w of L, w(a₀) ∏_i max(w(β_i), 1) = 1 (DT.0/finite-place-gauss-lemma).

Infinite places: for each embedding ψ : L → ℂ the ψ(β_i) are the complex roots of F_x (Polynomial.Splits.roots_map_of_injective), so a₀ ∏_i max(1, |ψ(β_i)|) = M(x) (Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_eq_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_roots). Grouping embeddings by infinite places (NumberField.InfinitePlace.card_filter_mk_eq) gives ∏_w (w(a₀) ∏_i max(w(β_i),1))^{mult w} = M(x)^{[L:ℚ]} (NumberField.Embeddings.card).

Multiply over all places: the factors w(a₀) multiply to 1 by the product formula (NumberField.prod_abs_eq_one), and the remaining factors are ∏_i mulHeight₁(β_i) computed in L (NumberField.mulHeight₁_eq). Hence ∏_i mulHeight₁(β_i) = M(x)^{[L:ℚ]}.
Each β_i has the minimal polynomial of x, so mulHeight₁(β_i) = absMulHeight₁(β_i)^{[L:ℚ]} = absMulHeight₁(x)^{[L:ℚ]} (DT.0/abs-mul-height-eq-rpow, DT.0/abs-mul-height-eq-of-minpoly-eq).
Therefore absMulHeight₁(x)^{d[L:ℚ]} = M(x)^{[L:ℚ]}; both sides are positive, so absMulHeight₁(x)^d = M(x).
acceptance: x = 1/2: M = 2 and absMulHeight₁(1/2) = mulHeight₁(1/2) = 2, d = 1.

nodes.title: Dirichlet's theorem for systems of linear forms, derived from Minkowski
nodes.statement: Let m, n ≥ 1, let A = (a_ij) be a real m × n matrix, L_i(y) = ∑_j a_ij y_j, and let Q > 1 be real. Then there are y ∈ ℤ^n \ {0} and x ∈ ℤ^m with max_j |y_j| ≤ Q and |L_i(y) − x_i| ≤ Q^{-n/m} for i = 1, …, m. The case m = n = 1 is Evertse's Theorem 1.1 (with the Minkowski derivation of printed pp. 2-3), the case n = 1 gives the simultaneous Theorem 1.4(i), and the case m = 1 the linear-form version of Corollary 2.7(ii).
hypotheses: Q > 1 is used to exclude y = 0: then |x_i| ≤ Q^{-n/m} < 1 forces x = 0. For Q = 1 the conclusion still holds trivially (y = e₁, x_i the nearest integer to a_i1), but not through Minkowski.
Closed inequalities (≤) on both sides: this needs Minkowski's linear forms theorem in its boundary form, with ∏ A_i ≥ |det|, as Evertse's Corollary 2.6 states it.
proofSteps: Consider the m + n linear forms in (x, y) ∈ ℝ^{m+n}: L_i(y) − x_i (i ≤ m) and y_j (j ≤ n). Their matrix is block triangular with diagonal blocks −I_m and I_n, so its determinant is ±1.
Take the bounds A_i = Q^{-n/m} for the first m forms and Q for the last n; their product is Q^{-n}·Q^{n} = 1 ≥ |det| = 1.
Minkowski's linear forms theorem (Evertse Corollary 2.6; requested from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.1) gives (x, y) ∈ ℤ^{m+n} \ {0} with |L_i(y) − x_i| ≤ Q^{-n/m} and |y_j| ≤ Q.
If y = 0 then |x_i| ≤ Q^{-n/m} < 1, so x = 0, a contradiction; hence y ≠ 0.
acceptance: m = n = 1, α real, Q = 2: some 0 < |y| ≤ 2 has ‖yα‖ ≤ 1/2; for α = 1/3, y = 1 gives |1/3 − 0| ≤ 1/2.
For m = n = 1 the Minkowski body C_Q = {(x, y) : |x − αy| ≤ Q^{-1}, |y| ≤ Q} has area 4 = 2², independent of α and Q; this is why Minkowski applies with no slack.

Mathlib's pigeonhole Dirichlet Real.exists_int_int_abs_mul_sub_le is the case m = n = 1 with the sharper bound 1/(Q + 1) for integer Q; this node is the geometry-of-numbers route and the general system.

proofSteps: For each real Q > 1, DT.0/dirichlet-approximation-from-minkowski gives (y_Q, x_Q) with y_Q ≠ 0, max|y_{Q,j}| ≤ Q and |L_i(y_Q) − x_{Q,i}| ≤ Q^{-n/m} ≤ (max_j |y_{Q,j}|)^{-n/m}.
If only finitely many pairs occurred, one pair (y₀, x₀) with y₀ ≠ 0 would occur for arbitrarily large Q, forcing L_i(y₀) = x₀,i ∈ ℤ for all i, which the hypothesis forbids.

nodes.title: Dirichlet's simultaneous approximation theorem
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, α₁, …, αₙ ∈ ℝ and Q > 1 real. Then there is (x₁, …, xₙ, y) ∈ ℤ^{n+1} with 0 < y ≤ Q^n and |x_i − α_i y| ≤ Q^{-1} for i = 1, …, n.
hypotheses: Q > 1 real (not necessarily an integer); the bound on y is Q^n.
proofSteps: Apply DT.0/dirichlet-approximation-from-minkowski with m := n forms in one variable (the column matrix (α_i)) and with Q^n in place of Q: it gives y ≠ 0 with |y| ≤ Q^n and |α_i y − x_i| ≤ (Q^n)^{-1/n} = Q^{-1}.
Replace (x, y) by (−x, −y) if y < 0.
acceptance: n = 1 recovers Theorem 1.1 (without the coprimality, which Mathlib's Real.exists_rat_abs_sub_le_and_den_le provides in that case).

nodes.title: Infinitely many simultaneous approximations with exponent 1 + 1/n
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1 and α₁, …, αₙ ∈ ℝ, not all rational. Then there are infinitely many (x₁, …, xₙ, y) ∈ ℤ^{n+1} with y > 0, gcd(x₁, …, xₙ, y) = 1 and |α_i − x_i/y| ≤ y^{-1-1/n} for i = 1, …, n.
hypotheses: Not all α_i rational; if all are rational the statement fails (only finitely many reduced tuples approach α that well, since α itself is one of them).

The exponent 1 + 1/n cannot be improved in general: for real algebraic α with 1, α₁, …, αₙ linearly independent, Schmidt's Theorem 1.6 (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.2) shows 1 + 1/n + δ admits only finitely many solutions.
proofSteps: The hypothesis of DT.0/dirichlet-linear-forms-infinitely-many holds for the m = n forms α_i y in the single variable y: α_i y ∈ ℤ for all i with y ≠ 0 would make all α_i rational.
It yields infinitely many (y, x) with y ≠ 0 and |α_i y − x_i| ≤ |y|^{-1/n}; change signs so that y > 0 and divide by y: |α_i − x_i/y| ≤ y^{-1-1/n}.
Divide (x, y) by g = gcd(x₁, …, xₙ, y): the ratios x_i/y are unchanged and y/g ≤ y, so the inequality persists.
Infinitely many reduced tuples remain: otherwise finitely many ratio vectors r would carry solutions with y → ∞, and |α_i − r_i| ≤ y^{-1-1/n} → 0 would make α = r rational.
acceptance: n = 1 gives Evertse's Corollary 1.2 (Mathlib's Real.infinite_rat_abs_sub_lt_one_div_den_sq_of_irrational, with strict inequality).
α = (√2, 1/2): infinitely many coprime (x₁, x₂, y) with |√2 − x₁/y|, |1/2 − x₂/y| ≤ y^{-3/2}.

nodes.title: The irrationality criterion by good integer approximations
nodes.statement: Let α ∈ ℝ and let (x_k, y_k) be integers with y_k > 0, x_k/y_k ≠ α and |x_k − αy_k| → 0 as k → ∞. Then α is irrational.
proofSteps: If α = a/b with b > 0, then for x/y ≠ α, |x − αy| = |bx − ay|/b ≥ 1/b, since bx − ay is a nonzero integer; this contradicts |x_k − αy_k| → 0.
acceptance: α = e with y_k = k!, x_k = k!∑_{j≤k} 1/j! (Evertse Theorem 1.10, DT.3).

nodes.title: Kronecker's approximation theorem
nodes.statement: Let α₁, …, αₙ, θ₁, …, θₙ ∈ ℝ and suppose that 1, α₁, …, αₙ are linearly independent over ℚ. Then for every ε > 0 there are infinitely many (x₁, …, xₙ, y) ∈ ℤ^{n+1} with |α_i y − x_i − θ_i| ≤ ε for i = 1, …, n.
hypotheses: The linear independence cannot be dropped: if a₁α₁ + ⋯ + aₙαₙ = a₀ with integers a_i not all zero, choose θ with a₁θ₁ + ⋯ + aₙθₙ ∉ ℤ at distance δ from ℤ; then the inequalities are unsolvable for ε < δ/∑|a_i|.
proofSteps: Let M be a large integer and L_M ⊂ ℝ^{n+1} the lattice of vectors (x₁ − α₁y, …, xₙ − αₙy, y/M), (x, y) ∈ ℤ^{n+1}; its polar is L*_M = {(x₁, …, xₙ, M(α₁x₁ + ⋯ + αₙxₙ + y))}.

Put R := C_{n+1}/ε with C_{n+1} the constant of the covering bound. Let μ > 0 be the minimum of |α₁x₁ + ⋯ + αₙxₙ + y| over the finitely many nonzero (x, y) with |x_i| < R and |α·x + y| ≤ 1 (positive by linear independence). For M ≥ max(R/μ, R), every nonzero polar vector has a coordinate of absolute value ≥ R.

The covering bound (Evertse Corollary 2.21, requested from GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic:GN.4, in the maximum-norm form with a constant C_{n+1} depending only on n) gives u ∈ L_M with every coordinate of u − b at most ε in absolute value, where b := (−θ₁, …, −θₙ, 2ε). Writing u from (x, y): |x_i − α_i y + θ_i| ≤ ε, i.e. |α_i y − x_i − θ_i| ≤ ε, and |y/M − 2ε| ≤ ε, so y ≥ Mε.

Since M can be taken arbitrarily large, y is unbounded and there are infinitely many solutions. (The source takes b = (θ₁, …, θₙ, 2Mε); its own next display needs b = (−θ₁, …, −θₙ, 2ε); recorded in sourceIssues.)
acceptance: n = 1: for irrational α the multiples yα are dense modulo 1 (the one-dimensional case).
α = (√2, √3) with 1, √2, √3 independent: for every (θ₁, θ₂) and ε > 0 some y makes y√2 and y√3 simultaneously ε-close to θ₁ and θ₂ modulo 1.

nodes.title: λ(θ) ≥ 1/n: the Dirichlet lower bound for simultaneous approximation
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 1 and θ ∈ ℝ^n, λ(θ) ≥ 1/n (DT.0/simultaneous-approximation-exponent); in particular λ_n(ξ) ≥ 1/n for every real ξ.
hypotheses: No hypothesis: if all θ_j are rational then λ(θ) = ∞.
proofSteps: If every θ_j is rational, multiples of a common denominator are exact solutions, so λ(θ) = ∞.
Otherwise DT.0/simultaneous-dirichlet-infinitely-many gives infinitely many (x, y) with y > 0 and |yθ_j − x_j| ≤ y^{-1/n}, i.e. the defining inequality with λ = 1/n and x₀ = y.

nodes.title: w(θ) ≥ n: the Dirichlet lower bound for a linear form
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1 and θ ∈ ℝ^n with 1, θ₁, …, θₙ linearly independent over ℚ. Then w(θ) ≥ n (DT.0/linear-form-exponent); in particular Mahler's w_n(ξ) ≥ n for every real ξ that is not algebraic of degree ≤ n.
hypotheses: Linear independence makes the linear form nonzero at every nonzero integer point, which the definition requires.
proofSteps: DT.0/dirichlet-linear-form-infinitely-many gives infinitely many (x, y), y ≠ 0, with |θ·y − x| ≤ ‖y‖^{-n}; by independence the value is nonzero.
|x| ≤ |θ·y| + 1 ≤ (1 + ∑|θ_j|)‖y‖, so the full vector (−x, y) has norm ≤ C‖y‖ with C = 1 + ∑|θ_j|; hence |form| ≤ C^n ‖(−x, y)‖^{-n}.
For every w < n the constant is absorbed for all but finitely many solutions, so ofReal w ≤ w(θ); take the supremum over w < n.
For θ = (ξ, …, ξⁿ): 1, ξ, …, ξⁿ are ℚ-linearly independent exactly when ξ is not algebraic of degree ≤ n.
acceptance: w(√2) ≥ 1 (and in fact = 1).

nodes.title: w*_n(ξ) ≤ w_n(ξ)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1 and ξ ∈ ℝ not algebraic of degree ≤ n. Then w*_n(ξ) ≤ w_n(ξ) (DT.0/algebraic-approximation-exponent, DT.0/linear-form-exponent).
hypotheses: ξ not algebraic of degree ≤ n, so P(ξ) ≠ 0 for every nonzero P ∈ ℤ[X] of degree ≤ n.
proofSteps: Let α be algebraic of degree ≤ n with 0 < |ξ − α| ≤ min(1, H(α)^{-w-1}). Take P = F_α, of degree ≤ n with H(P) = H(α) (DT.0/naive-height-of-algebraic-number).

By the mean value inequality on the segment [α, ξ] ⊂ ℂ (Convex.norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_deriv_le), |P(ξ)| = |P(ξ) − P(α)| ≤ |ξ − α|·max_{[α,ξ]} |P'| ≤ c(n, ξ)·H(α)·|ξ − α| ≤ c(n, ξ)·H(P)^{-w}, and P(ξ) ≠ 0.
Infinitely many α give infinitely many P, since each P has at most n roots (Polynomial.card_roots'); the constant c(n, ξ) is absorbed by any smaller exponent. Hence w_n(ξ) ≥ w − δ for all δ > 0.
acceptance: n = 1: both sides equal μ(ξ) − 1 for irrational ξ.

nodes.title: Lower bound for the error of a convergent
nodes.statement: Let ξ be irrational with convergents p_k/q_k (Mathlib's Real.convergent ξ k, in lowest terms). Then |ξ − p_k/q_k| > 1/(q_k(q_k + q_{k+1})) for every k ≥ 0. Together with Mathlib's upper bound |ξ − p_k/q_k| ≤ 1/(q_k q_{k+1}) this pins the error within a factor 2.
hypotheses: ξ irrational, so the continued fraction does not terminate.
proofSteps: GenContFract.sub_convs_eq: ξ − A_k/B_k = (−1)^k / (B_k(r⁻¹B_k + B_{k−1})) with r ∈ (0, 1) the k-th fractional part, whose inverse r⁻¹ < a_{k+1} + 1.
Since B_{k+1} = a_{k+1}B_k + B_{k−1}, the denominator is < B_k(B_{k+1} + B_k).
A_k/B_k = Real.convergent ξ k (Real.convs_eq_convergent) and B_k is its reduced denominator (the determinant formula GenContFract.determinant makes A_k, B_k coprime).

sources.match: Formula (iv) gives our bound, which is sharper than the lower half of (v) since q_{k+2} ≥ q_{k+1} + q_k.

nodes.title: The irrationality exponent from the continued fraction: μ(ξ) = 1 + limsup log q_{k+1}/log q_k
nodes.statement: Let ξ be irrational with convergent denominators q_k. Then μ(ξ) = 1 + limsup_{k→∞} log q_{k+1} / log q_k (in ℝ≥0∞, the finitely many k with q_k = 1 contributing 0). Equivalently μ(ξ) = 2 + limsup log a_{k+1}/log q_k with a_k the partial quotients.
hypotheses: ξ irrational (for rational ξ the expansion terminates and μ = 1).
proofSteps: Write |ξ − p_k/q_k| = q_k^{-λ_k}. By DT.0/convergent-error-lower-bound and Mathlib's upper bound (GenContFract.abs_sub_convs_le), 1/(2q_kq_{k+1}) < |ξ − p_k/q_k| ≤ 1/(q_kq_{k+1}), so λ_k = 1 + log q_{k+1}/log q_k + O(1/log q_k).

Any rational r with |ξ − r| < 1/(2 den(r)²) is a convergent (Legendre, Real.exists_rat_eq_convergent); hence for exponents p > 2 the rational approximations of order p are, apart from finitely many, convergents, and μ(ξ) = max(2, limsup λ_k) = limsup λ_k (using λ_k ≥ 2).
q_k → ∞, so the O(1/log q_k) term vanishes in the limsup; combine with DT.0/irrationality-exponent (API irrationalityExponent_eq_iSup_infinite).
The second form follows from q_{k+1} = a_{k+1}q_k(1 + o(1))-type bounds a_{k+1}q_k ≤ q_{k+1} ≤ (a_{k+1} + 1)q_k.
acceptance: Golden ratio: q_k = F_{k+1} (Fibonacci), log q_{k+1}/log q_k → 1, μ = 2.
Liouville-type expansions with a_{k+1} ≥ q_k^k give μ = ∞.

nodes.title: The binary form of a root controls the distance to a rational point (Evertse (6.2))
nodes.statement: Let f ∈ ℤ[X] have degree d ≥ 1 and let α ∈ ℂ be a root of f. Write F(X, Y) = Y^d f(X/Y) = ∑_{k} f_k X^k Y^{d-k} for the homogenization of f in degree d (Mathlib's Polynomial.homogenize f d). For all integers x and y with y > 0: |F(x, y)| ≤ 2^{d-1} M(f) max(|x|, y)^d |α − x/y|, where M(f) is the Mahler measure of f viewed in ℂ[X]. When gcd(x, y) = 1, max(|x|, y) = H(x/y).
hypotheses: f ∈ ℤ[X], d = deg f ≥ 1
α ∈ ℂ with f(α) = 0
x ∈ ℤ, y ∈ ℤ with y > 0 (no coprimality needed for the inequality)
proofSteps: Over ℂ, f = a_0 ∏_{i=1}^{d} (X − α_i) with α_1 = α, a_0 the leading coefficient (Polynomial.C_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_multiset_X_sub_C with IsAlgClosed.card_roots_eq_natDegree); hence F(x, y) = a_0 ∏_i (x − α_i y).
M(f) = |a_0| ∏_i max(1, |α_i|) (Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_eq_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_roots).
For i ≥ 2: |x − α_i y| ≤ |x| + |α_i| y ≤ 2 max(1, |α_i|) max(|x|, y).
For i = 1: |x − α y| = y |α − x/y| ≤ max(1, |α|) max(|x|, y) |α − x/y|.
Multiply the d factors and the leading coefficient: |F(x, y)| ≤ 2^{d-1} |a_0| ∏_i max(1, |α_i|) max(|x|, y)^d |α − x/y| = 2^{d-1} M(f) max(|x|, y)^d |α − x/y|.
acceptance: The inequality is an equality-free, effective bound: every constant is computable from f; it is reused by the effective improvement of Liouville (Evertse, proof of Theorem 6.5).

nodes.title: Liouville's inequality with the explicit constant 2^{1-d} M(α)^{-1} (Evertse, Theorem 6.1)
nodes.statement: Let α ∈ ℂ be algebraic of degree d ≥ 1 with primitive minimal polynomial F_α ∈ ℤ[X] (irreducible, primitive, positive leading coefficient) and Mahler measure M(α) = M(F_α). For every ξ ∈ ℚ with ξ ≠ α: |ξ − α| ≥ 2^{1-d} M(α)^{-1} H(ξ)^{-d}, where H(x/y) = max(|x|, |y|) for coprime x, y (Mathlib's mulHeight₁ on ℚ). The constant is effectively computable from α.
hypotheses: α algebraic over ℚ of degree d ≥ 1 (α may be non-real)
F_α the primitive minimal polynomial; M(α) its Mahler measure (stage DT.0)
ξ ∈ ℚ, ξ ≠ α
proofSteps: Write ξ = x/y with gcd(x, y) = 1, y > 0, so H(ξ) = max(|x|, y) (Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max).
F(x, y) := y^d F_α(x/y) is an integer. It is nonzero: if d = 1 the only root of F_α is α ≠ ξ; if d ≥ 2, F_α is irreducible of degree ≥ 2 over ℚ and has no rational root. Hence |F(x, y)| ≥ 1.
Apply binary-form-distance-bound with f = F_α: 1 ≤ |F(x, y)| ≤ 2^{d-1} M(α) H(ξ)^d |α − ξ|; rearrange.
acceptance: Degree 1: α = a/b rational gives |ξ − α| ≥ M(α)^{-1} H(ξ)^{-1} = 1/(max(|a|, b) H(ξ)), consistent with |a/b − x/y| ≥ 1/(by).

Compatibility with Mathlib's Liouville.exists_pos_real_of_irrational_root: for irrational real α the explicit constant is an admissible value of that theorem's existential constant (up to the (b+1) versus H(ξ) normalisation).
Effectivity: M(α) is computable from F_α, so the lower bound is explicit, in contrast with Thue's and Roth's theorems in this stage.

nodes.title: Thue's auxiliary polynomials (Evertse, Lemma 6.10)
nodes.statement: Let α ∈ ℂ be algebraic of degree d, b ≥ 1 an integer with bα ∈ O_{ℚ(α)} (for instance the leading coefficient of the primitive minimal polynomial), and 0 < ε < 1/2. For every integer r ≥ 1 there are P_r, Q_r ∈ ℤ[X], not both 0, of degree at most m := [(1/2 + ε) d r], such that (X − α)^r divides P_r − α Q_r in ℂ[X] and ‖P_r‖, ‖Q_r‖ ≤ C_1^r with C_1 = (12 b max(1, house α))^{d(1 + 1/ε)}; C_1 depends only on α and ε and is effectively computable. (Evertse's proof bounds the largest coefficient by (6 b max(1, house α))^{d(1 + 1/ε) r}; the extra factor 2^{d(1+1/ε)} absorbs the at most m + 1 ≤ 2^{dr} coefficients of the ℓ¹-norm.)
hypotheses: α algebraic of degree d ≥ 1
proofSteps: Unknowns: the 2m + 2 integer coefficients of P_r = ∑ p_i X^i, Q_r = ∑ q_i X^i.
(X − α)^r | P_r − αQ_r iff P_r^{((k))}(α) − α Q_r^{((k))}(α) = 0 for k = 0..r−1 (Taylor expansion at α, Polynomial.taylor_coeff).

Multiply the k-th equation by b^m: ∑_i binom(i, k) b^m α^{i−k} p_i − ∑_i binom(i, k) b^m α^{i−k+1} q_i = 0, r equations with coefficients in O_K, K = ℚ(α), [K : ℚ] = d, of house ≤ A := (2b max(1, house α))^{(2+2ε)dr}.
Since 2m + 2 > (1 + 2ε)dr > dr, siegel-lemma-with-algebraic-integer-coefficients gives a nonzero integer solution with max |p_i|, |q_i| ≤ (3(2m+2)A)^{dr/(2m+2−dr)} ≤ (3(2+2ε)drA)^{1/(2ε)}.

Using 3(2+2ε)dr ≤ 3^{(2+2ε)dr}, every coefficient is at most (6b max(1, house α))^{d(1+1/ε) r} (the source's final display); summing the at most m + 1 ≤ 2^{dr} ≤ 2^{d(1+1/ε) r} coefficients gives ‖P_r‖, ‖Q_r‖ ≤ C_1^r.
acceptance: d = 3, ε = 1/4, r = 4: m = 9 and 20 unknowns against 4 equations over a cubic field (20 > 12).
The divisibility is by the power of X − α, not by a power of the minimal polynomial: P_r − αQ_r has non-rational coefficients.

sources.locator: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.10 with proof, printed p. 119
sources.excerpt: Lemma 6.10. For every positive integer r there exist polynomials P_r, Q_r ∈ Z[X] of degree at most [(1/2 + ε)dr], not both equal to 0, with the following properties: P_r − αQ_r is divisible by (X − α)^r, ∥P_r∥ ⩽ C_1^r, ∥Q_r∥ ⩽ C_1^r
sources.match: Statement and proof; the source's C_1 = (6b max(1, house α))^{d(1+ε^{-1})} bounds the coefficients, and the node doubles its base to bound the ℓ¹-norm (gap recorded).

nodes.title: A power of a linear factor forces the same power of the minimal polynomial (Evertse, Lemma 6.11)

hypotheses: β algebraic over ℚ
F ∈ ℚ[X]
proofSteps: Induction on m. f | F since F(β) = 0 (minpoly.dvd) when m ≥ 1.
β is a simple root of f (f is irreducible over a field of characteristic 0, hence separable), so (X − β)^{m−1} divides F/f in ℂ[X]; apply the induction hypothesis to F/f ∈ ℚ[X].

nodes.title: A divided derivative of bounded order does not vanish at two rationals (Evertse, Lemma 6.12)
nodes.statement: Let α be algebraic of degree d ≥ 2, 0 < ε < 1/2, r ≥ 1, and P_r, Q_r ∈ ℤ[X], not both 0, of degree ≤ (1/2 + ε)dr with (X − α)^r | P_r − αQ_r. For all ξ_1, ξ_2 ∈ ℚ there is an integer k with 0 ≤ k ≤ d(2εr + 1) and P_r^{((k))}(ξ_1) ≠ ξ_2 Q_r^{((k))}(ξ_1).
hypotheses: α irrational algebraic of degree d ≥ 2 (the source assumes d ≥ 3)
P_r, Q_r as produced by thue-auxiliary-polynomials
proofSteps: Put F := P_r Q_r' − P_r' Q_r (Mathlib's wronskian P_r Q_r). F ≠ 0: otherwise P_r/Q_r (say Q_r ≠ 0) is a constant c ∈ ℚ, c ≠ α, and Q_r = (c − α)^{-1}(P_r − αQ_r) is divisible by (X − α)^r, hence by f^r (minimal-polynomial-power-divides), impossible since rd > (1/2 + ε)dr ≥ deg Q_r.

Suppose P_r^{((k))}(ξ_1) = ξ_2 Q_r^{((k))}(ξ_1) for k = 0..t. Eliminating ξ_2 gives P^{((k))}Q^{((l))} − P^{((l))}Q^{((k))} = 0 at ξ_1 for k, l ≤ t; by the Leibniz rule (Polynomial.hasseDeriv_mul) F^{((k))} is a combination of these for l, m ≤ k + 1, so F^{((k))}(ξ_1) = 0 for k ≤ t − 1 and (X − ξ_1)^t | F.
F = Q_r'(P_r − αQ_r) − Q_r(P_r' − αQ_r') is divisible by (X − α)^{r−1}, hence by f^{r−1} (minimal-polynomial-power-divides); f and X − ξ_1 are coprime, so (X − ξ_1)^t f^{r−1} | F.
deg F ≤ (1 + 2ε)dr − 1 (Polynomial.natDegree_wronskian_lt_add), so t ≤ d(2εr + 1) − 1; hence the equality fails for some k ≤ t + 1 ≤ d(2εr + 1).
acceptance: The bound is k ≤ d(2εr + 1) (not <): the source's subsequent use of k < d(2εr + 1) is recorded as a misprint.
The identity for F uses the factors P_r − αQ_r and P_r' − αQ_r'; the source prints Q_r' − αP_r' and Q_r − αP_r (misprint recorded).

sources.locator: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.12 with proof, printed pp. 120-121
sources.excerpt: Lemma 6.12. Let ξ1, ξ2 be two rational numbers, and r a positive integer. Then there is k ⩽ d(2εr + 1) such that P_r^{((k))}(ξ1) ≠ ξ2 Q_r^{((k))}(ξ1). Proof. The proof rests upon an analysis of the polynomial F := P_r Q'_r − P'_r Q_r.
sources.match: Statement and proof, with the identity for F corrected.

nodes.title: Bounds for the remainder and the derivative at a close rational (Evertse, Lemma 6.13)
nodes.statement: Let α ∈ ℂ, d ≥ 1, ε > 0, C_1 ≥ 0, integers 0 ≤ k ≤ r, and P, Q ∈ ℤ[X] of degree ≤ (1/2 + ε)dr with ‖P‖, ‖Q‖ ≤ C_1^r. Write P^{((k))} − αQ^{((k))} = V (X − α)^{r−k} with V ∈ ℂ[X]. Then for every z ∈ ℂ with |z − α| ≤ 1: |V(z)| ≤ C_2^r and |Q^{((k))}(z)| ≤ C_2^r, where C_2 = 2^{(1/2+ε)d} (1 + |α|)^{1+(1/2+ε)d} C_1.
hypotheses: 0 ≤ k ≤ r
degree and norm bounds as produced by thue-auxiliary-polynomials
|z − α| ≤ 1 (in the application z = ξ_1 is a solution of |ξ − α| ≤ H(ξ)^{-κ})
proofSteps: Put P̃(X) = P^{((k))}(X + α), Q̃(X) = Q^{((k))}(X + α), Ṽ(X) = V(X + α), z̃ = z − α; then P̃ − αQ̃ = X^{r−k} Ṽ, so Ṽ has the coefficients of P̃ − αQ̃.
By l1-norm-taylor-shift-bound and l1-norm-hasse-derivative-bound: ‖P̃‖ ≤ (2(1+|α|))^{(1/2+ε)dr} C_1^r, and likewise ‖Q̃‖; by l1-norm-add-le: ‖Ṽ‖ ≤ (1 + |α|)(2(1+|α|))^{(1/2+ε)dr} C_1^r ≤ C_2^r.
Since |z̃| ≤ 1, l1-norm-eval-bound gives |Q^{((k))}(z)| = |Q̃(z̃)| ≤ ‖Q̃‖ ≤ C_2^r and |V(z)| = |Ṽ(z̃)| ≤ ‖Ṽ‖ ≤ C_2^r.
acceptance: C_2 depends only on α, ε, C_1 (hence on α, κ, ε) and is effectively computable.
The hypothesis k ≤ r is what makes V a polynomial; in the proof of Theorem 6.9 it follows from (6.21) (recorded as a gap in the source).

sources.locator: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.13 with proof, printed pp. 121-122
sources.excerpt: Lemma 6.13. There is an effectively computable number C2 depending only on α, κ and ε such that |V_r(ξ1)| ⩽ C2^r, |Q_r^{((k))}(ξ1)| ⩽ C2^r. ... with C2 := 2^{(1/2+ε)d}(1 + |α|)^{1+(1/2+ε)d}C1.
sources.match: Statement and proof, stated for any polynomials with the degree and norm bounds of Lemma 6.10.

nodes.title: Thue's method as an effective gap principle (Evertse, Theorem 6.14 and the proof of Theorem 6.9)
nodes.statement: Let α ∈ ℂ be algebraic of degree d ≥ 2 and κ > d/2 + 1. There are effectively computable C ≥ 1 and λ ≥ 1, depending only on α and κ, such that: if ξ_1 ∈ ℚ satisfies |ξ_1 − α| ≤ H(ξ_1)^{-κ} and H(ξ_1) ≥ C, then every other ξ ∈ ℚ with |ξ − α| ≤ H(ξ)^{-κ} satisfies H(ξ) ≤ H(ξ_1)^λ. One may take ε = (κ − 1 − d/2)/((2κ + 2)d), C = max(e, (2C_2)^{2/(εd)}) and λ = 1 + 2(1 + κd)/(dε), with C_2 as in thue-remainder-bounds for C_1 as in thue-auxiliary-polynomials.
hypotheses: α algebraic of degree d ≥ 2 (the source says 'of degree d'; the proof needs α ∉ ℚ, recorded as a gap)
heights are H(x/y) = max(|x|, |y|) for coprime x, y
proofSteps: Fix ε as stated; then 0 < ε < 1/2 and (1/2 + ε)d + 1 − κ + 2κεd = −εd.
Suppose ξ_1, ξ_2 are solutions with H(ξ_1) ≥ C and H(ξ_2) > H(ξ_1)^λ (so H(ξ_2) > e H(ξ_1)); set r = ⌊log H(ξ_2)/log H(ξ_1)⌋ ≥ 2(1 + κd)/(dε) ≥ 1.

Take P_r, Q_r from thue-auxiliary-polynomials. For 0 ≤ k ≤ d(2εr + 1) (note d(2εr + 1) ≤ r by the size of r) put A_{r,k} := y_1^{[(1/2+ε)dr]} y_2 (P_r^{((k))}(ξ_1) − ξ_2 Q_r^{((k))}(ξ_1)) ∈ ℤ, where ξ_i = x_i/y_i in lowest terms.
By thue-nonvanishing-of-a-divided-derivative some A_{r,k} ≠ 0, so |A_{r,k}| ≥ 1.

Since r ≥ 2(1 + κd)/(dε), both exponents are ≤ −εdr/2, and H(ξ_1) ≥ (2C_2)^{2/(εd)} gives |A_{r,k}| ≤ 2C_2^r H(ξ_1)^{-εdr/2} ≤ 2^{1−r} < 1 (r ≥ 2), a contradiction. Hence every solution ξ ≠ ξ_1 has H(ξ) ≤ H(ξ_1)^λ.
acceptance: The two-solution structure is the source of ineffectivity in Theorem 6.9: C is explicit, but nothing guarantees a solution of height ≥ C is known.
Evertse, Exercise 6.8(iv): together with the elementary gap principle this bounds the number of solutions explicitly.

sources.excerpt: Let ξ1, ξ2 be two solutions of (6.10) with H(ξ2) > e · H(ξ1) and define the integer r by r ⩽ log H(ξ2)/log H(ξ1) < r + 1. ... we choose solutions ξ1, ξ2 of (6.10) such that (6.21) H(ξ1) ⩾ (2C2)^{2/εd}, log H(ξ2)/log H(ξ1) ⩾ 1 + 2(1 + κd)/(dε)

There are effectively computable positive numbers C, λ depending on α, κ, such that if ξ1 is a solution of (6.10) |ξ − α| ⩽ H(ξ)^{−κ} in ξ ∈ Q with H(ξ1) ⩾ C, then for any other solution ξ of (6.10) we have H(ξ) ⩽ H(ξ1)^λ.

nodes.title: Thue's approximation theorem (Evertse, Theorem 6.9)
nodes.statement: Let α be a real algebraic number of degree d ≥ 3 and κ > d/2 + 1. Then |ξ − α| ≤ H(ξ)^{-κ} has only finitely many solutions ξ ∈ ℚ. The proof does not provide the solutions (ineffective).
hypotheses: α real algebraic of degree d ≥ 3
H(ξ) = max(|x|, |y|) for ξ = x/y in lowest terms
proofSteps: Suppose there are infinitely many solutions. By Northcott over ℚ (NumberField.finite_setOfPred_mulHeight₁_le) there is a solution ξ_1 with H(ξ_1) ≥ C (C, λ from thue-effective-gap-principle), and then a solution ξ_2 with H(ξ_2) > H(ξ_1)^λ.
This contradicts thue-effective-gap-principle.
acceptance: d = 3: every κ > 5/2 is admissible; Roth improves this to κ > 2. d = 4: κ > 3.
The argument needs two solutions ξ_1, ξ_2 with H(ξ_2) much larger than H(ξ_1); it bounds the number of solutions but not their size (ineffectivity, Evertse p. 110).
Thue's proof does not use Liouville's inequality.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 6.9. Let α be a real algebraic number of degree d ⩾ 3 and κ > d/2 + 1. Then the inequality (6.10) |ξ − α| ⩽ H(ξ)^{−κ} in ξ ∈ Q has only finitely many solutions.
sources.match: Exact statement.

sources.excerpt: In contrast, the results of Thue, Siegel, Gel’fond, Dyson and Roth mentioned above are ineffective, i.e., with their methods of proof one can prove only the existence of a constant c(α, κ) > 0 as in (6.3), but one can not compute such a constant.
sources.match: The ineffectivity recorded in the statement.

nodes.title: Divided (Hasse) partial derivatives of multivariate polynomials
nodes.statement: For a commutative semiring R, a type σ of variables and d ∈ ℕ^(σ) (finitely supported), the R-linear map ∂^d on R[x_σ] with ∂^d(x^m) = (∏_j binom(m_j, d_j)) x^{m−d} (and 0 when some d_j > m_j). Over a ring containing ℚ, ∂^d = (∏_j d_j!)^{-1} ∂^{|d|}/∂x^d; over ℤ it preserves integrality.
hypotheses: R a commutative semiring (ℤ, ℚ, ℝ, number fields in the applications)
d finitely supported
proofSteps: Define ∂^d on the monomial basis by the displayed formula and extend linearly (sum over the support of P).

nodes.title: The index of a polynomial at a point with respect to weights
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, weights r ∈ ℕ^σ, a point a ∈ R^σ and P ∈ R[x_σ]: Ind_{a,r}(P) := min { ∑_j i_j / r_j : i ∈ ℕ^(σ), (∂^i P)(a) ≠ 0 } ∈ [0, ∞], with Ind_{a,r}(0) = ∞. Equivalently, Ind_{a,r}(P) ≥ t iff ∂^i P(a) = 0 for every i with ∑_j i_j/r_j < t. For P ≠ 0 and all r_j ≥ 1 it is a finite rational number.
hypotheses: R a commutative ring
weights r_j ≥ 1 for the finiteness and characterisation lemmas
value in [0, ∞] (ℝ≥0∞), ∞ exactly at P = 0
proofSteps: Define as the infimum in [0, ∞] of the weights ∑_j i_j/r_j over the i with (∂^i P)(a) ≠ 0 (the empty infimum is ∞).

sources.excerpt: Definition 2.6.2. For points α = (α1, . . . , αn) ∈ C^n, and r = (r1, . . . , rn) ∈ N^n, we define for all P ∈ C[x1, . . . , xn] \ {0} the index of P with respect to α and r to be Ind(α,r)(P) = min{ i1/r1 + . . . + in/rn | (i1, . . . , in) ∈ N_0^n and ∂(i1,...,in)P(α) ≠ 0}.

nodes.title: The index is additive (Pottmeyer, Exercise 2.19)
nodes.statement: Over an integral domain R with all r_j ≥ 1: Ind_{a,r}(PQ) = Ind_{a,r}(P) + Ind_{a,r}(Q) for all P, Q (with ∞ + x = ∞).
hypotheses: R an integral domain
r_j ≥ 1
proofSteps: By multivariate-taylor-expansion, Ind_{a,r}(P) is the least weight w(i) = ∑_j i_j/r_j of a monomial y^i occurring in P(a + y).
The lowest-weight parts (sums of the terms of minimal weight) of P(a + y) and Q(a + y) multiply to the lowest-weight part of the product, which is nonzero in a domain; w is additive.

nodes.title: The index under a divided derivative
nodes.statement: Over an integral domain of characteristic 0: Ind_{a,r}(P) ≤ Ind_{a,r}(∂^d P) + ∑_j d_j/r_j.

nodes.title: The projective height of a multivariate polynomial
nodes.statement: For a field K with admissible absolute values (a number field in the applications) and P ∈ K[x_σ]: h(P) := the logarithmic projective height of the coefficient vector of P, i.e. Mathlib's Finsupp.logHeight of the coefficient function. For a number field K and P ≠ 0: h(P) = ∑_{w | ∞} mult(w) log max_m w(coeff_m P) + ∑_{v ∤ ∞} log max_m v(coeff_m P). It is the relative height over K; Pottmeyer's absolute h_P(P) is h(P)/[K : ℚ]. Over ℚ, for P ∈ ℤ[x] with coprime coefficients, h(P) = log max_m |coeff_m P|.

vars(P) ∩ vars(Q) = ∅
proofSteps: Monomials of PQ are the products of monomials of P and of Q, bijectively (the variables are disjoint), so the coefficient vector of PQ is the multiplication table (p_a q_b); apply Height.mulHeight_fun_mul_eq and take logarithms.

nodes.title: The height of an integer polynomial is at most the log of its largest coefficient
nodes.statement: For P ∈ ℤ[x_σ], P ≠ 0, viewed over ℚ: h(P) ≤ log max_m |coeff_m P|, with equality when the coefficients are coprime.
hypotheses: P ≠ 0 with integer coefficients
proofSteps: Divide by the content c: h(P) = h(P/c) (projectivity) = log max |coeff(P/c)| (Rat.mulHeight_eq_max_abs_of_gcd_eq_one) = log(max|coeff P|/c) ≤ log max|coeff P|.

nodes.title: Products of central binomial coefficients (Pottmeyer, Lemma 3.2.8)
nodes.statement: For a, b ∈ ℕ: binom(a, ⌊a/2⌋) binom(b, ⌊b/2⌋) ≤ binom(a + b, ⌊(a + b)/2⌋).
hypotheses: a, b ≥ 0
proofSteps: The coefficient of x^{⌊a/2⌋ + ⌊b/2⌋} in (1 + x)^a (1 + x)^b is ∑_{k+l} binom(a,k) binom(b,l) ≥ binom(a,⌊a/2⌋) binom(b,⌊b/2⌋), and every coefficient of (1 + x)^{a+b} is at most the central one.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.2.8. Let r1, . . . , rn ∈ N0 be arbitrary. Then we have (r1 choose ⌊r1/2⌋) · · · (rn choose ⌊rn/2⌋) ⩽ (r1 + . . . + rn choose ⌊(r1 + . . . + rn)/2⌋).

nodes.title: Central binomial coefficient times √(d + 1) (Pottmeyer, Lemma 3.2.9)
nodes.statement: For d ∈ ℕ: binom(d, ⌊d/2⌋) √(d + 1) ≤ 2^d.
proofSteps: Check d = 0, 1; for even d = 2d' induct on d' using binom(2d'+2, d'+1) = binom(2d', d') (2d'+1)(2d'+2)/(d'+1)^2 and (2d'+1)^2 (2d'+3) ≤ 4(d'+1)^2(2d'+1)... ; deduce odd d from even d − 1 via binom(d, ⌊d/2⌋) = binom(d−1, ⌊(d−1)/2⌋) · d/⌈d/2⌉ (the source leaves the details as Exercise 3.4).

nodes.title: The archimedean Gelfond inequality in one variable (Pottmeyer, Lemma 3.2.10 for n = 1)
nodes.statement: For f, g ∈ ℂ[X]: |f| |g| ≤ 2^{deg(fg)} |fg|, where |·| is the largest absolute value of a coefficient (Mathlib's supNorm).
hypotheses: f, g ∈ ℂ[X]
proofSteps: |f| ≤ binom(deg f, ⌊deg f/2⌋) M(f) and |g| ≤ binom(deg g, ⌊deg g/2⌋) M(g) (Polynomial.supNorm_le_choose_natDegree_div_two_mul_mahlerMeasure).
M(f)M(g) = M(fg) (Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_mul) ≤ √(deg(fg) + 1) |fg| (Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_le_sqrt_natDegree_add_one_mul_supNorm).
Combine with central-binomial-product-le and central-binomial-sqrt-bound (deg(fg) = deg f + deg g for f, g ≠ 0; trivial otherwise).

nodes.title: Gelfond's lemma in one variable (Pottmeyer, Proposition 3.2.12)
nodes.statement: For a number field K and nonzero f, g ∈ K[X]: h(f) + h(g) ≤ h(fg) + [K : ℚ] deg(fg) log 2 (relative heights over K).
hypotheses: K a number field
f, g ≠ 0
proofSteps: At a finite place v, max_i v(coeff) is multiplicative (Gauss's lemma, Polynomial.gaussNorm_mul with c = 1).
At an infinite place w with embedding σ (NumberField.InfinitePlace.embedding), apply complex-sup-norm-product-bound to σ(f), σ(g): log w(f) + log w(g) ≤ log w(fg) + deg(fg) log 2.
Sum with the multiplicities w.mult, whose total is [K : ℚ] (NumberField.totalWeight_eq_finrank), using the place-by-place formula of height-of-one-variable-polynomial.
acceptance: Pottmeyer's multivariable form (all partial degrees) is not needed in this stage: Roth's lemma uses Gelfond only in one variable.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 3.2.12 (Gelfond’s Lemma). Let f1, . . . , fr ∈ Q̄[x1, . . . , xn], and define f = f1 · · · fr. Then we have HP(f) ⩾ 2^{−(degx1(f)+...+degxn(f))} Π_{j=1}^{r} HP(fj).

nodes.title: Roth's lemma in one variable (Pottmeyer, Lemma 3.4.3)
nodes.statement: For a number field K, P ∈ K[X] \ {0}, an integer r ≥ deg P and β ∈ K: ord_β(P) h(β) ≤ h(P) + [K : ℚ] r log 2 (relative heights over K). Consequently, if r h(β) ≥ σ^{-1}(h(P) + 4r[K : ℚ]) with 0 < σ, then Ind_{β,r}(P) = ord_β(P)/r ≤ σ (Remark 3.4.4).
hypotheses: deg P ≤ r
β ∈ K
proofSteps: Write P = (X − β)^m P' with m = ord_β(P) (Polynomial.pow_rootMultiplicity_dvd).
gelfond-lemma-one-variable: h(P) ≥ h((X − β)^m) + h(P') − [K:ℚ] r log 2.
h(P') ≥ 0, and h((X − β)^m) ≥ m h(β): at each place the maximum over the coefficients binom(m, i)(−β)^i is at least max(1, |β^m|_v) (take i = 0, m) and ∑ log max(1, |β|^m_v) = m h(β).
For the consequence divide by r h(β) (positive by the hypothesis) and use weighted-index-one-variable.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.4.3. Let P ∈ Q̄[x] \ {0}, r ⩾ deg(P) ∈ N, and β ∈ Q̄ be arbitrary. Then Ind_{r,β}(P) · r · h(β) = ord_β(P) · h(β) ⩽ hP(P) + r log(2).

nodes.title: The Wronskian criterion (Pottmeyer, Proposition 3.3.3)
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and g_1, ..., g_m ∈ K[X]. Then g_1, ..., g_m are K-linearly independent iff W(g_1, ..., g_m) ≠ 0.
hypotheses: K of characteristic 0 (false in characteristic p: W(1, X^p) = 0)
proofSteps: Dependent ⇒ W = 0: a linear relation among the columns persists after differentiation (Lemma 3.3.2).

W = 0 ⇒ dependent, by induction on m: if W(g_1..g_{m−1}) = 0 use the induction hypothesis; otherwise the columns of the m × m matrix are dependent over K(X): ∑ c_l g_l^{((k))} = 0 for k < m with c_m = 1, c_l ∈ K(X).

Differentiating the relation for k < m − 1 and subtracting (k + 1)× the relation for k + 1 (using D g^{((k))} = (k + 1) g^{((k+1))}) gives ∑_l c_l' g_l^{((k))} = 0 for k < m − 1, a relation among the first m − 1 columns (c_m' = 0) with nonzero minor W(g_1..g_{m−1}); hence all c_l' = 0.
In characteristic 0 an element of K(X) with zero derivative lies in K, so ∑ c_l g_l = 0 is a K-linear relation.
acceptance: The characteristic-0 hypothesis cannot be dropped: over 𝔽_p, 1 and X^p are independent but the classical Wronskian vanishes.

nodes.title: Kronecker substitution preserves linear independence (Pottmeyer, Exercise 3.5(a))
nodes.statement: Let K be a field, f_1..f_m ∈ K[x_1..x_n] and B > every partial degree of every f_l. Then f_1..f_m are linearly independent iff the one-variable polynomials φ(f_l) = f_l(t, t^B, ..., t^{B^{n−1}}) are.
hypotheses: B > deg_{x_i} f_l for all i, l
proofSteps: The substitution x^a ↦ t^{a_1 + a_2 B + ... + a_n B^{n−1}} is injective on exponents with a_i < B (base-B digits), so φ is an injective linear map on the span of the monomials occurring.
acceptance: n = 2, B = 2: x_0 and x_1 go to t and t^2.

sources.excerpt: (a) Prove that the polynomials f1, . . . , fm are F-linearly independent, if and only if the polynomials ϕ(f1), . . . , ϕ(fm) are linearly independent.
sources.match: The exercise that fills the gap in the proof of Theorem 3.3.7.

nodes.title: Derivatives of a Kronecker substitution (Pottmeyer, Exercise 3.5(b))
nodes.statement: For n, B, k there are polynomials a_{d,k} ∈ K[t], zero unless |d| ≤ k, such that for every f ∈ K[x_1..x_n]: (d/dt)^k φ(f) = ∑_d a_{d,k}(t) φ(∂^d f), where φ(f) = f(t, t^B, ..., t^{B^{n−1}}).
hypotheses: K a field (any characteristic)
proofSteps: Induction on k with the chain rule: d/dt φ(g) = ∑_i B^{i−1} t^{B^{i−1}−1} φ(∂g/∂x_i); rewrite products of ordinary partial derivatives through divided ones (multivariate-hasse-derivative, factorial_smul_hasseDeriv_single); the coefficients do not depend on f.
acceptance: n = 1, B = 1: φ = id and a_{(k),k} = k!.

sources.excerpt: (b) Let k ∈ N0 be arbitrary, and set g^{(k)} as the kth derivative of g ∈ F[x]. Prove that there are polynomials a_{d,k} ∈ F[t] such that for all i ∈ {1, . . . , m} we have ϕ(fi)^{(k)} = Σ_{ord(∂d)⩽k} a_{d,k} ∂_d fi(t, t^d, . . . , t^{d^{n−1}}).
sources.match: The exercise.

nodes.title: The generalized Wronskian criterion (Pottmeyer, Theorem 3.3.7)
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and f_1..f_m ∈ K[x_1..x_n]. Then f_1..f_m are linearly independent iff some admissible generalized Wronskian W_D(f) (|D_k| ≤ k, 0-indexed) is nonzero.
hypotheses: K of characteristic 0
proofSteps: If dependent, every W_D vanishes (a column relation persists under ∂^{D_k}).
If independent, choose B larger than all partial degrees; by kronecker-substitution-linear-independence the φ(f_l) are independent, so their Wronskian is nonzero (wronskian-criterion-one-variable).

By kronecker-substitution-derivatives each row k of the classical Wronskian of the φ(f_l) is a K[t]-combination of the rows φ(∂^d f_l) with |d| ≤ k; by multilinearity of the determinant, W(φ(f)) is a K[t]-combination of the φ(W_D(f)) over admissible D. Hence some W_D(f) ≠ 0.
acceptance: n = 1 recovers the Wronskian criterion (only D_k = k e_1 gives a nonzero determinant).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 3.3.7. The polynomials f1, . . . , fm ∈ F[x1, . . . , xn] are F-linearly independent if and only if there is some generalized Wronskian determinant W_{d(1),...,d(m)}(f1, . . . , fm) not identically zero.
sources.match: Statement and proof (with Exercise 3.5 supplying the omitted steps).

nodes.title: Separating one variable (Pottmeyer, Lemma 3.3.8)
nodes.statement: Let K be a field, P ∈ K[x_σ] \ {0} and i_0 ∈ σ. There are s ≤ deg_{x_{i_0}} P, linearly independent f_0..f_s not involving x_{i_0}, and linearly independent g_0..g_s involving only x_{i_0}, with P = ∑_{k=0}^{s} f_k g_k.
proofSteps: P = ∑_{i ≤ r} f'_i x_{i_0}^i is such a decomposition with independent g_i = x_{i_0}^i; take one with s minimal among those with g independent.
If the f_k were dependent, f_s = ∑_{k<s} c_k f_k gives P = ∑_{k<s} f_k (g_k + c_k g_s) with independent g_k + c_k g_s, contradicting minimality.
acceptance: P = x_0 x_1 + x_0: s = 0, f_0 = x_0, g_0 = x_1 + 1 (separating x_1).

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.3.8. For any P ∈ F[x1, . . . , xn] \ {0} there are F-linearly independent polynomials f0, . . . , fs ∈ F[x1, . . . , xn−1], and F-linearly independent polynomials g0, . . . , gs ∈ F[xn], such that P(x1, . . . , xn) = Σ_{i=0}^{s} fi(x1, . . . , xn−1) · gi(xn), where s ⩽ degxn(P).
sources.match: Statement and proof, for any distinguished variable.

nodes.title: The Wronskian factorisation (Pottmeyer, Lemma 3.3.9)
nodes.statement: Let f_0..f_s not involve x_{i_0}, g_0..g_s involve only x_{i_0}, P = ∑ f_k g_k, and D_0..D_s with (D_k)_{i_0} = 0. Then W_D(f) · W_{(0, e_{i_0}, ..., s e_{i_0})}(g) = det(∂^{D_k + l e_{i_0}} P)_{0 ≤ k, l ≤ s}.
hypotheses: f_k free of x_{i_0}
g_k in x_{i_0} only
D_k supported off i_0
proofSteps: det(A) det(B) = det(A B^T) with A = (∂^{D_k} f_j), B = (∂^{l e_{i_0}} g_j).
(A B^T)_{k,l} = ∑_j ∂^{D_k} f_j ∂^{l e_{i_0}} g_j = ∂^{D_k + l e_{i_0}}(∑_j f_j g_j) by the Leibniz rule, since the variables are separated (multivariate-hasse-derivative).
acceptance: s = 0: f_0 g_0 = P and W = P.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.3.9. Let P(x1, . . . , xn) = Σ_{i=0}^{s} fi(x1, . . . , xn−1) · gi(xn) ∈ F[x1, . . . , xn] be as in Lemma 3.3.8. Moreover, let W_{d(0),...,d(s)}(f0, . . . , fs) be any generalized Wronskian determinant of f0, . . . , fs. Then, W(f)·W_{0,1,...,s}(g) = det(∂_{(d(i),j)}P)
sources.match: Statement and proof, with the index misprints corrected (recorded).

nodes.title: Coefficients of a product under any absolute value (Pottmeyer, Remark 3.2.11)
nodes.statement: For an absolute value v on an integral domain R, finitely many f_k ∈ R[x_1..x_n] and a monomial m: v(coeff_m ∏_k f_k) ≤ 2^{∑_j deg_{x_j}(∏_k f_k)} ∏_k max_a v(coeff_a f_k).
hypotheses: v an absolute value (triangle inequality suffices)
R an integral domain (so partial degrees add)
proofSteps: coeff_m ∏ f_k is a sum over decompositions m = ∑_k a_k of ∏_k coeff_{a_k} f_k; there are at most ∏_k ∏_j (deg_{x_j} f_k + 1) ≤ ∏_j 2^{∑_k deg_{x_j} f_k} = 2^{∑_j deg_{x_j} ∏ f_k} such terms.
acceptance: (1 + x)^r: the middle coefficient binom(r, r/2) ≤ 2^r.

sources.excerpt: Remark 3.2.11. A straight forward computation, which we avoid in this lecture, also gives the estimate |f1| · · · |fr| ⩾ 2^{−(degx1(f)+...+degxn(f))} |f|, with the notation from Lemma 3.2.10.
sources.match: The remark, with the omitted computation supplied in the proof steps and stated for any absolute value.

nodes.title: Height of a determinant of derivatives of one polynomial (Pottmeyer, §3.4.6)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, P ∈ K[x_1..x_n] and E_{k,l} ∈ ℕ^n (0 ≤ k, l < m). Then h(det(∂^{E_{k,l}} P)) ≤ m h(P) + [K : ℚ](2m (∑_j deg_{x_j} P) log 2 + log m!). In particular, under Roth's-lemma hypothesis (ii) and s ≤ r_n (m = s + 1, deg_{x_j} P ≤ r_j), h(W) ≤ (s + 1)(h(P) + 4 r_1 [K : ℚ]) ((3.19)).
hypotheses: K a number field
any matrix of divided derivatives of one polynomial
proofSteps: Leibniz formula (Matrix.det_apply): a sum of m! products of m entries.

At a finite place: each coefficient of ∂^E P is ≤ max v(coeff P) (hasse-derivative-nonarchimedean-coefficient-bound); products and sums obey the ultrametric bounds (MvPowerSeries.gaussNorm_mul_le, IsNonarchimedean.apply_sum_le).

At an infinite place: each entry has max coefficient ≤ 2^{∑ deg} max v(coeff P) (hasse-derivative-archimedean-coefficient-bound), a product of m entries has partial degrees ≤ m deg_{x_j} P, so product-coefficient-bound contributes 2^{m ∑ deg}; the sum contributes m!.
Sum the logarithms over the places with multiplicities (total weight [K : ℚ], NumberField.totalWeight_eq_finrank).
acceptance: The source's intermediate archimedean factor 2^{r_1+...+r_n} should be 2^{(s+1)(r_1+...+r_n)}; the final bound (3.21) is unaffected (recorded).

sources.excerpt: We combine all these estimates to achieve hP(W) ⩽ (s + 1)hP(P) + log(2^{(s+1)(r1+...+rn)}) + log(2^{r1+...+rn}) + log((s + 1)!) ... ⩽ (s + 1)(hP(P) + 2(r1 + . . . + rn) log(2) + log((s + 1)!)/(s + 1)) (3.21)
sources.match: The estimate (3.21) for any matrix of derivatives, with the archimedean factor corrected.

nodes.title: A lower bound for truncated linear sums (Pottmeyer, Lemma 3.4.8)
nodes.statement: For k ∈ ℕ and δ ∈ ℝ: ∑_{i=0}^{k} max(δ − i/k, 0) ≥ (k + 1) min(δ/2, δ^2/2) (with i/0 := 0).
hypotheses: k ≥ 0, δ real
proofSteps: δ ≤ 0: the left side is 0 and the right side is ≤ 0.
δ ≥ 1: all terms are positive and the sum is (k + 1)(δ − 1/2) ≥ (k + 1)δ/2.
0 < δ < 1, k ≥ 1: with c = ⌈δk⌉ the sum is cδ − c(c − 1)/(2k), a concave function of c ∈ [δk, δk + 1] whose values at both ends equal kδ^2/2 + δ/2 ≥ (k + 1)δ^2/2. k = 0: the sum is max(δ, 0) ≥ δ/2.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 3.4.8. Let k ∈ N0 and δ ∈ R be arbitrary, then Σ_{i=0}^{k} max{δ − i/k, 0} ⩾ (k + 1) · min{1/2 δ, 1/2 δ^2}.
sources.match: Statement; the proof (an exercise in the source) is supplied.

nodes.title: Roth's lemma (Pottmeyer, Theorem 3.4.1)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, n ≥ 1, P ∈ K[x_1..x_n] \ {0}, β ∈ K^n, 0 < σ ≤ 1/2 and r ∈ ℕ^n with r_i ≥ 1, such that (i) deg_{x_i} P ≤ r_i; (ii) r_{i+1} ≤ σ r_i for 1 ≤ i < n; (iii) r_i h(β_i) ≥ σ^{-1}(h(P) + 4 n r_1 [K : ℚ]) for all i (relative heights over K). Then Ind_{β,r}(P) ≤ 2n σ^{1/2^{n−1}}.
hypotheses: K a number field; heights relative to K (Pottmeyer's absolute form is the case of dividing (iii) by [K : ℚ])
r_i ≥ 1
proofSteps: Induction on n. n = 1: roth-lemma-one-variable gives Ind ≤ σ ≤ 2σ.
n ≥ 2: separation-of-one-variable (separating x_n) gives P = ∑_{k=0}^{s} f_k g_k with s ≤ r_n, f independent in x_1..x_{n−1}, g independent in x_n.

generalized-wronskian-criterion gives an admissible D with U := W_D(f) ≠ 0; wronskian-criterion-one-variable gives V := W(g) ≠ 0; wronskian-factorisation-for-separated-variables gives W := UV = det(∂^{D_k + l e_n} P).

Put r' = (s + 1) r. U and V satisfy (i) for r' (degreeOf_genWronskian_le) and (ii) trivially. By generalized-wronskian-height-bound and height-of-product-in-disjoint-variables, h(U) + h(V) = h(W) ≤ (s + 1)(h(P) + 4r_1[K : ℚ]), which gives (iii) for U (in n − 1 variables, (3.17)) and for V ((3.18)).

Induction hypothesis for U (weighted-index-rename) and roth-lemma-one-variable for V, with weighted-index-scale-weights: Ind_{β,r}(U) ≤ 2(s + 1)(n − 1)σ^{1/2^{n−2}} and Ind_{β,r}(V) ≤ (s + 1)σ; by weighted-index-mul, Ind_{β,r}(W) ≤ 2(s + 1)(n − 1)σ^{1/2^{n−2}} + (s + 1)σ.

Lower bound: by the Leibniz formula, weighted-index-add and weighted-index-mul, Ind(W) ≥ min_π ∑_i Ind(∂^{(D_i, π(i))} P); by weighted-index-of-derivative with |D_i| ≤ s ≤ r_n and r_n/r_{n−1} ≤ σ, Ind(∂^{(D_i, π(i))} P) ≥ max(Ind(P) − π(i)/r_n, 0) − σ; summing over the permutation and applying truncated-linear-sum-lower-bound (with i/r_n ≤ i/s) gives Ind(W) ≥ (s + 1) min(Ind(P)/2, Ind(P)^2/2) − (s + 1)σ.

Compare: min(Ind(P), Ind(P)^2) ≤ 4(n − 1)σ^{1/2^{n−2}} + 4σ; since Ind(P) ≤ n (weighted-index-le-sum-degreeOf and (i)), Ind(P)^2 ≤ 4n(n − 1)σ^{1/2^{n−2}} + 4nσ ≤ 4n^2 σ^{1/2^{n−2}}, so Ind(P) ≤ 2nσ^{1/2^{n−1}}.
acceptance: n = 1 is roth-lemma-one-variable.
The lemma is nontrivial only for small σ (Ind ≤ n always).
Applied in this stage with K = ℚ and β_i rational approximations of α; stated over any number field because the source proves it for algebraic points and the proof is uniform.

sources.locator: Theorem 3.4.1 and its proof 3.4.3-3.4.8, printed pp. 90-94
sources.excerpt: Theorem 3.4.1 (Roth’s Lemma). ... (i) ri ⩾ degxi(P) for all i ∈ {1, . . . , n}, (ii) ri+1 ⩽ ri · σ for all i ∈ {1, . . . , n − 1}, and (iii) rih(βi) ⩾ σ^{−1}(hP(P) + 4nr1) for all i ∈ {1, . . . , n}. Then, we have Ind_{r,β}(P) ⩽ 2nσ^{1/2^{n−1}}.
