Then at least one of the (d_0 + d_1)n numbers y_{hj} (1 ≤ h ≤ d_0, 1 ≤ j ≤ n) and e^{x_i·y_j} (1 ≤ i ≤ d_1, 1 ≤ j ≤ n) is transcendental. Proposed declaration: Baker.schneiderLang_cartesian.
hypotheses: x_i ∈ ℚ̄^n, ℚ-linearly independent
(y_j) a ℂ-basis of ℂ^n
proofSteps: Suppose all these numbers are algebraic; let K be the number field they generate together with the coordinates of the x_i (Setting SL).

Parameter choice (Step 6): fix a large integer S_1; let T range over n-th powers that are multiples of S_1^n, and put T_0 = T_1 = T, S_0 := c_0T^{d/n}/S_1, E := S_0^{(d−n)/d}, E' := S_0'^{(d−n)/d}. Then (4.15), (4.17), (4.18) hold for large T because d/n > 1.

DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/schneider-lang-auxiliary-function-vanishing gives F, and DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/schneider-lang-extrapolation-upper-bound gives log|D^{σ^0}F(s^0y)| ≤ −(S_0'S_1/(2n)) log E' + c_9S_0' log S_0' + c_10(T_0 log(S_1E') + T_1S_1E').
DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/schneider-lang-liouville-lower-bound gives log|D^{σ^0}F(s^0y)| ≥ −c_1(N + S_0' log T_1 + T_0 log(S_1 + S_0') + T_1S_1).
With the choices above the upper bound is smaller than the lower bound for T large (condition (4.19) with c_11 enlarged by the factor 2n): contradiction.

nodes.title: Waldschmidt Corollary 4.3 (the case d_0 = 0)
nodes.statement: Let x_1, …, x_d ∈ ℚ̄^n generate a subgroup of rank ≥ n + 1 and let {y_1, …, y_ℓ} ⊆ ℂ^n contain a basis of ℂ^n. Then at least one of the dℓ numbers x_i·y_j (1 ≤ i ≤ d, 1 ≤ j ≤ ℓ) does not belong to 𝓛. Proposed declaration: Baker.schneiderLang_homogeneous.

the y_j span ℂ^n
proofSteps: Choose n + 1 of the x_i that are ℚ-linearly independent and n of the y_j forming a basis. If all x_i·y_j ∈ 𝓛, all e^{x_i·y_j} are algebraic, contradicting DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/schneider-lang-cartesian-products with d_0 = 0, d_1 = n + 1.

(y_j) a basis

nodes.title: Bertrand-Masser: a relation Σ β_iℓ_i ∈ ℚ̄ with a ℚ-basis (β_i) of a number field forces ℓ = 0 (Waldschmidt Theorem 4.5)
nodes.statement: Let K ⊆ ℂ be a number field of degree d, (β_1, …, β_d) a basis of K over ℚ, and ℓ_1, …, ℓ_d ∈ 𝓛 with β_1ℓ_1 + ⋯ + β_dℓ_d ∈ ℚ̄. Then ℓ_1 = ⋯ = ℓ_d = 0. Proposed declaration: Baker.eq_zero_of_isAlgebraic_sum_basis_mul.
hypotheses: (β_k) a ℚ-basis of K
ℓ_k ∈ 𝓛
Σ β_kℓ_k algebraic
proofSteps: Let σ_1 = id, σ_2, …, σ_d be the embeddings K → ℂ and λ_i := Σ_k σ_i(β_k)ℓ_k. The matrix B = (σ_i(β_k)) is invertible: det(B)² is the discriminant of the basis (Algebra.discr_eq_det_embeddingsMatrixReindex_pow_two), which is nonzero (Algebra.discr_not_zero_of_basis) — Waldschmidt's Lemma 4.6.

Case 1, some but not all λ_i vanish, say λ_1, …, λ_n ≠ 0 = λ_{n+1} = ⋯ = λ_d: x_i := (σ_1(β_i), …, σ_n(β_i)) ∈ ℚ̄^n are ℚ-linearly independent, y_j := (σ_1(β_j)λ_1, …, σ_n(β_j)λ_n) contain a basis of ℂ^n, and x_i·y_j = Σ_k Tr(β_iβ_jβ_k)ℓ_k ∈ 𝓛 (traces are rational); this contradicts DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/schneider-lang-homogeneous-corollary.

Case 2, no λ_i vanishes: x_k := (σ_1(β_k), …, σ_d(β_k)), y_j := (σ_1(β_j)λ_1, …, σ_d(β_j)λ_d) form a basis, y_{1j} = β_jλ_1 is algebraic (λ_1 = Σ β_kℓ_k ∈ ℚ̄), and x_i·y_j ∈ 𝓛 as before; this contradicts DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/schneider-lang-inhomogeneous-corollary.
Case 3: all λ_i = 0; since B is invertible, ℓ = 0.
acceptance: K = ℚ(∛2), β = (1, ∛2, ∛4): ℓ_1 + ∛2ℓ_2 + ∛4ℓ_3 = 0 with ℓ_i ∈ 𝓛 forces ℓ_i = 0 (the special case of §4.2.1).

nodes.title: Baker's theorem: ℚ-linearly independent logarithms of algebraic numbers are linearly independent over ℚ̄ together with 1
nodes.statement: Let λ_1, …, λ_m ∈ 𝓛 be linearly independent over ℚ. Then 1, λ_1, …, λ_m are linearly independent over ℚ̄: if β_0, β_1, …, β_m are algebraic and β_0 + β_1λ_1 + ⋯ + β_mλ_m = 0 then β_0 = β_1 = ⋯ = β_m = 0. (Evertse Theorem 5.1: for α_i ∈ ℚ̄ \ {0, 1}, any logarithms log α_i that are ℚ-linearly independent, γ ∈ ℚ̄ and nonzero β_i ∈ ℚ̄: γ + β_1 log α_1 + ⋯ + β_m log α_m ≠ 0; DALAG Theorem 1.6.) Proposed declaration: Transcendence.linearIndependent_cons_one_of_linearIndependent_rat.
hypotheses: λ_i ∈ 𝓛 (arbitrary logarithms, no branch condition)
λ ℚ-linearly independent
proofSteps: Let γ_0 + Σ γ_jλ_j = 0 with γ_j algebraic. Put K := ℚ(γ_1, …, γ_m) ⊆ ℂ, choose a ℚ-basis (β_1, …, β_d) of K and write γ_j = Σ_i c_{ji}β_i with c_{ji} ∈ ℚ.
Then Σ_i β_iℓ'_i = −γ_0 ∈ ℚ̄ with ℓ'_i := Σ_j c_{ji}λ_j ∈ 𝓛 (a ℚ-subspace); DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/baker-theorem-number-field-basis gives ℓ'_i = 0.
By ℚ-linear independence of the λ_j, all c_{ji} = 0; hence γ_1 = ⋯ = γ_m = 0 and then γ_0 = 0.
acceptance: λ = (log 2, log 3): 1, log 2, log 3 are ℚ̄-linearly independent, so √2 log 2 + log 3 is transcendental.
The hypothesis is ℚ-linear independence of the chosen logarithms: λ_1 = log 2, λ_2 = log 2 + 2πi are ℚ-independent (Waldschmidt's warning, CIME Theorem 3.1) and the theorem applies to them.
The ℚ-linear dependence of logarithms is decidable only through the multiplicative dependence of the α_i up to 2πi: the hypothesis must be verified at each use.

nodes.statement: Let λ_1, …, λ_n ∈ 𝓛 be linearly independent over ℚ and β_1, …, β_n nonzero algebraic numbers. Then β_1λ_1 + ⋯ + β_nλ_n is transcendental. Proposed declaration: Transcendence.transcendental_sum_mul_of_linearIndependent.

β_i algebraic, nonzero
proofSteps: If γ := Σ β_iλ_i were algebraic, (−γ) + Σ β_iλ_i = 0 would be a nontrivial ℚ̄-linear relation among 1, λ_1, …, λ_n (β_1 ≠ 0), contradicting DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/baker-linear-independence-of-logarithms.

nodes.title: Transcendence of α_1^{β_1}⋯α_n^{β_n} (Evertse Corollary 4.20)
nodes.statement: Let α_1, …, α_n be nonzero algebraic numbers that are multiplicatively independent, λ_i any logarithms of α_i (λ_i ∈ 𝓛, e^{λ_i} = α_i), and β_1, …, β_n algebraic with (β_1, …, β_n) ∉ ℚ^n. Then α_1^{β_1}⋯α_n^{β_n} := e^{β_1λ_1+⋯+β_nλ_n} is transcendental. Proposed declaration: Transcendence.transcendental_exp_sum_mul.
hypotheses: α_i ≠ 0 algebraic, multiplicatively independent
λ_i ∈ 𝓛 with e^{λ_i} = α_i
β ∈ ℚ̄^n \ ℚ^n
proofSteps: Multiplicative independence implies the λ_i are ℚ-linearly independent: an integer relation Σx_iλ_i = 0 gives ∏α_i^{x_i} = 1.

Suppose α_{n+1} := e^{Σβ_iλ_i} is algebraic and put λ_{n+1} := Σβ_iλ_i ∈ 𝓛. By DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/baker-linear-independence-of-logarithms (with coefficients (1, −β)), λ_1, …, λ_{n+1} are ℚ-linearly dependent: Σ_{i≤n+1} x_iλ_i = 0 with x ∈ ℤ^{n+1} \ {0}; x_{n+1} ≠ 0 by the first step.

Eliminating λ_{n+1}: Σ_i (x_{n+1}β_i + x_i)λ_i = 0 with some coefficient nonzero because β ∉ ℚ^n; DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/baker-linear-independence-of-logarithms again contradicts the ℚ-independence of λ_1, …, λ_n.
acceptance: n = 1 is the Gelfond-Schneider theorem for α_1 not a root of unity.

nodes.title: Waldschmidt's measure of linear independence of logarithms (DALAG Theorem 9.1 with C(m) = 2^{m+25}m^{3m+9})
nodes.statement: Let m ≥ 1 and C(m) := 2^{m+25}m^{3m+9}. Let λ_1, …, λ_m ∈ 𝓛 be linearly independent over ℚ, α_j := e^{λ_j}, and β_0, …, β_m algebraic numbers, not all zero; D := [ℚ(α_1, …, α_m, β_0, …, β_m) : ℚ]. Let B, E, E* ≥ e and A_1, …, A_m > 0 be reals with log A_j ≥ max{h(α_j), E|λ_j|/D, (log E)/D}, log E* ≥ max{(1/D) log E, log(D/log E)}, B ≥ E*, and either (i) B ≥ max_i (D log A_i)/(log E) and log B ≥ max_{0≤i≤m} h(β_i), or (ii) β_0 = 0, β_i = b_i ∈ ℤ, b_m ≠ 0 and B ≥ max_{1≤j<m}(|b_m|/log A_j + |b_j|/log A_m)(log E)/D. Then Λ := β_0 + β_1λ_1 + ⋯ + β_mλ_m ≠ 0 and |Λ| > exp{−C(m)D^{m+2}(log B)(log A_1)⋯(log A_m)(log E*)(log E)^{−m−1}}. Heights: h(α) is the absolute logarithmic Weil height (Mathlib NumberField.absLogHeight₁) and H_abs(α) = e^{h(α)} (NumberField.absMulHeight₁); for a rational x/y in lowest terms H_abs = max(|x|, |y|) (Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max). Evertse's naive height H (DT.0/naive-height-of-algebraic-number) satisfies 2^{−d}H(α) ≤ H_abs(α)^d ≤ √(d+1)·H(α) for α of degree d (DT.0/height-comparisons). Proposed declaration: LogarithmicForms.waldschmidt_measure.

β not all zero, algebraic
parameter inequalities (i) or (ii)

nodes.title: Baker's lower bound for linear forms in logarithms (Evertse Theorem 5.2)
nodes.statement: Let m ≥ 1, let λ_1, …, λ_m ∈ 𝓛 (arbitrary logarithms of nonzero algebraic numbers, not assumed ℚ-linearly independent) and D ≥ 1. There is C > 0, depending only on m, D and λ_1, …, λ_m, such that for all algebraic γ, β_1, …, β_m of degree ≤ D with Λ := γ + β_1λ_1 + ⋯ + β_mλ_m ≠ 0: |Λ| ≥ (eB)^{−C}, where B := max(H_abs(γ), H_abs(β_1), …, H_abs(β_m)). With Evertse's naive height H in place of H_abs the statement is equivalent (C changes by a factor depending only on D; DT.0/height-comparisons). C is effectively computable: the proof gives it explicitly from C(m) of DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/waldschmidt-linear-independence-measure. Heights: h(α) is the absolute logarithmic Weil height (Mathlib NumberField.absLogHeight₁) and H_abs(α) = e^{h(α)} (NumberField.absMulHeight₁); for a rational x/y in lowest terms H_abs = max(|x|, |y|) (Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max). Evertse's naive height H (DT.0/naive-height-of-algebraic-number) satisfies 2^{−d}H(α) ≤ H_abs(α)^d ≤ √(d+1)·H(α) for α of degree d (DT.0/height-comparisons). Proposed declaration: LogarithmicForms.baker_lower_bound.
hypotheses: λ_i ∈ 𝓛
deg γ, deg β_i ≤ D
Λ ≠ 0 (essential: nothing is claimed when Λ = 0)
proofSteps: Reduction to independent logarithms: the subgroup M := ℤλ_1 + ⋯ + ℤλ_m of 𝓛 is finitely generated and torsion-free, hence free with a basis μ_1, …, μ_k ∈ 𝓛 (k ≤ m), ℚ-linearly independent; λ_i = Σ_j n_{ij}μ_j with fixed n_{ij} ∈ ℤ, and Λ = γ + Σ_j β'_jμ_j with β'_j := Σ_i n_{ij}β_i.
Heights and degrees: deg β'_j ≤ D^m and h(β'_j) ≤ Σ_i (h(β_i) + log|n_{ij}|) + m log 2 ≤ m log B + c (elementary height inequalities for the absolute height; see the gap on the absolute-height API).
k = 0: Λ = γ ≠ 0 and |γ| ≥ H_abs(γ)^{−D} ≥ (eB)^{−D}, since |γ^{−1}| ≤ M(γ^{−1}) = H_abs(γ)^{deg γ} (DT.0/height-comparisons and h(γ^{−1}) = h(γ)).

k ≥ 1: apply DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/waldschmidt-linear-independence-measure, case (i), to μ_1, …, μ_k and (γ, β'_1, …, β'_k), with E := e, fixed A_j and E* depending only on the μ_j and the degree bound, and log B' := max(m log(eB) + c, D' log A_j, log E*): it gives |Λ| > exp(−c' log B') ≥ (eB)^{−C}.
acceptance: γ = 0, β_i = b_i ∈ ℤ: the homogeneous rational case used for DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/baker-lower-bound-for-multiplicative-form.
The branch of each λ_i is part of the data: replacing λ_1 by λ_1 + 2πi changes Λ and C.
B is a height of the coefficients; the dependence on the α_i = e^{λ_i} is inside C.

nodes.title: Lower bound for |α_1^{b_1}⋯α_m^{b_m} − 1| (Evertse Corollary 5.3)
nodes.statement: Let α_1, …, α_m be nonzero algebraic numbers. There is C' > 0, depending only on m and α_1, …, α_m (through their degrees and heights), such that for all b ∈ ℤ^m with α_1^{b_1}⋯α_m^{b_m} ≠ 1: |α_1^{b_1}⋯α_m^{b_m} − 1| ≥ (eB)^{−C'}, B := max|b_i|. No choice of logarithm enters the statement; the proof uses the principal logarithm Complex.log. Proposed declaration: LogarithmicForms.baker_lower_bound_prod_sub_one.
hypotheses: α_i ≠ 0 algebraic (Evertse also excludes α_i = 1, which is harmless)
α^b ≠ 1
proofSteps: Let z := α^b − 1 ≠ 0 (so B ≥ 1). If |z| > 1/2 the bound holds for C' ≥ 1. Assume |z| ≤ 1/2.
With the principal logarithm, e^{log(1+z)} = 1 + z = e^{Σ b_j log α_j}, so log(1 + z) = Σ b_j log α_j + 2k·πi for some k ∈ ℤ (Complex.exp_eq_exp_iff_exists_int), and log(1 + z) ≠ 0.
|log(1 + z)| ≤ (3/2)|z| ≤ 1 (Complex.norm_log_one_add_half_le_self), hence |2kπ| ≤ 1 + Σ|b_j||log α_j| ≤ C_2B with C_2 := 1 + Σ|log α_j|.

Apply DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/baker-lower-bounds-for-linear-forms-in-logarithms to the m + 1 logarithms log α_1, …, log α_m, πi ∈ 𝓛 with integer coefficients (degree 1, heights ≤ max(B, |2k|) ≤ C_2B): |log(1 + z)| ≥ (eC_2B)^{−C_1}, so |z| ≥ (2/3)(eC_2B)^{−C_1} ≥ (eB)^{−C'}.
acceptance: The hypothesis α^b ≠ 1 is necessary: for α = (2, 4), b = (2, −1) the form vanishes.

nodes.title: Matveev's explicit lower bound for linear forms in logarithms (Matveev 2000, Corollary 2.3)
nodes.statement: Let K ⊆ ℂ be a number field of degree D; κ := 1 if K ⊆ ℝ and κ := 2 otherwise. Let α_1, …, α_n ∈ K^×, λ_1, …, λ_n NONZERO logarithms of them (λ_j ∈ 𝓛 \ {0}, e^{λ_j} = α_j, arbitrary branches), b_1, …, b_n ∈ ℤ and Λ := b_1λ_1 + ⋯ + b_nλ_n ≠ 0. Let A_j ≥ max{D·h(α_j), |λ_j|, 0.16} and B* := max|b_j| (or B := max{1, max_j |b_j|A_j/A_n}). Then log|Λ| > −C_1(n)·D²·A_1⋯A_n·log(eD)·log(eB*), where C_1(n) = C_1(n, κ) = min{(1/κ)(en/2)^κ·30^{n+3}·n^{3.5}, 2^{6n+20}}. Heights: h(α) is the absolute logarithmic Weil height (Mathlib NumberField.absLogHeight₁) and H_abs(α) = e^{h(α)} (NumberField.absMulHeight₁); for a rational x/y in lowest terms H_abs = max(|x|, |y|) (Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max). Evertse's naive height H (DT.0/naive-height-of-algebraic-number) satisfies 2^{−d}H(α) ≤ H_abs(α)^d ≤ √(d+1)·H(α) for α of degree d (DT.0/height-comparisons). Proposed declaration: LogarithmicForms.matveev.
hypotheses: λ_j ∈ 𝓛, λ_j ≠ 0, e^{λ_j} ∈ K
b ∈ ℤ^n, Λ ≠ 0
A_j ≥ max{D h(α_j), |λ_j|, 0.16}

nodes.title: Matveev's bound for rational numbers (Evertse Theorem 5.4, corrected constant)
nodes.statement: Let a_1, …, a_m be nonzero rational numbers and b ∈ ℤ^m with a_1^{b_1}⋯a_m^{b_m} ≠ 1; B := max|b_i|. Then |a_1^{b_1}⋯a_m^{b_m} − 1| ≥ (2/3)·(eB)^{−C'} with C' := (e/2)·m^{4.5}·30^{m+3}·∏_{j=1}^{m} max(1, log H(a_j)), where H(x/y) = max(|x|, |y|) in lowest terms. (Evertse prints |⋯ − 1| ≥ (eB)^{−C'}; the factor 2/3 is what the derivation from Matveev's Corollary 2.3 gives — see sourceIssues.) Proposed declaration: LogarithmicForms.matveev_rat.
hypotheses: a_j ∈ ℚ^×
a^b ≠ 1
proofSteps: Signs and units: if a^b < 0 then |a^b − 1| > 1. Otherwise a^b = ∏|a_j|^{b_j}; drop the j with |a_j| = 1. If nothing remains, a^b = ±1 ≠ 1 gives |a^b − 1| = 2. The bound for fewer terms implies the stated one (C' increases with m and with the factors).
If |Λ| > 1/2 the bound holds. Otherwise x := Σ b_j log|a_j| ∈ ℝ satisfies e^x = 1 + Λ, x = log(1 + Λ) ≠ 0 and |x| ≤ (3/2)|Λ| (Complex.norm_log_one_add_half_le_self).

Apply DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/matveev-corollary-linear-form-bound with K = ℚ (D = 1, κ = 1, log(eD) = 1), λ_j = log|a_j| ≠ 0, A_j := max(1, log H(a_j)) ≥ max{h(a_j), |log|a_j||, 0.16} (h(a_j) = log H(a_j) by Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max, and |log|x/y|| ≤ log max(|x|, |y|)), B* = B: C_1(m, 1) ≤ (em/2)30^{m+3}m^{3.5} = (e/2)m^{4.5}30^{m+3}, so |x| > (eB)^{−C'} and |Λ| ≥ (2/3)|x|.
acceptance: Negative a_j with small height (a_j = −1) are handled by the sign reduction, not by the formula.

If moreover L ⊆ ℝ, then log|Λ| > −1.4·30^{n+3}n^{4.5}D²(1 + log D)(1 + log B)A_1⋯A_n. Heights: h(α) is the absolute logarithmic Weil height (Mathlib NumberField.absLogHeight₁) and H_abs(α) = e^{h(α)} (NumberField.absMulHeight₁); for a rational x/y in lowest terms H_abs = max(|x|, |y|) (Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max). Evertse's naive height H (DT.0/naive-height-of-algebraic-number) satisfies 2^{−d}H(α) ≤ H_abs(α)^d ≤ √(d+1)·H(α) for α of degree d (DT.0/height-comparisons). hypotheses: α_j ∈ L^×
A_j ≥ max{D h(α_j), |log α_j|, 0.16}, principal log
proofSteps: If |Λ| ≥ 1/3 the bounds hold. Otherwise, with the principal logarithm, there is b_0 ∈ ℤ with |b_0| ≤ nB such that Ω := |b_0 log(−1) + Σ b_j log α_j| satisfies |Λ| ≥ Ω/2 (|log(1 + Λ)| ≤ (3/2)|Λ| and Complex.exp_eq_exp_iff_exists_int); b_0 = 0 if L ⊆ ℝ.

Drop the j with log α_j = 0. Apply DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.3/matveev-corollary-linear-form-bound to the n + 1 logarithms πi, log α_1, …, log α_n (A for −1: h′(−1) = π; κ ≤ 2), resp. to the n real logarithms (κ = 1), and compare constants: (e²/8)(n + 1)^{5.5}30^{n+4}·π ≤ 3·30^{n+4}(n+1)^{5.5} and (e/2) ≤ 1.4, the slack absorbing log 2.

nodes.title: Yu's explicit p-adic lower bound (Yu 1994, §0.1)
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, α_1, …, α_n nonzero algebraic numbers, K := ℚ(α_1, …, α_n) of degree d, p a prime, 𝔭 a prime ideal of 𝓞_K above p with residue degree f_𝔭, and ord_𝔭 the exponent of 𝔭 in a nonzero fractional ideal. Let b ∈ ℤ^n \ {0} with α_1^{b_1}⋯α_n^{b_n} ≠ 1, and reals h_1, …, h_n with h_j ≥ max(h(α_j), |log α_j|/(10d), log p) (log α_j with imaginary part in (−π, π], i.e. Complex.log). Then ord_𝔭(α_1^{b_1}⋯α_n^{b_n} − 1) < Φ·log(dB), where B := max(|b_1|, …, |b_n|, 3), h' := max(h_1, …, h_n, 1) and Φ := 22000·(9.5(n + 1)d/√(log p))^{2(n+1)}·(p^{f_𝔭} − 1)·h_1⋯h_n·log(10ndh'). No p-adic logarithm occurs in the statement. Heights: h(α) is the absolute logarithmic Weil height (Mathlib NumberField.absLogHeight₁) and H_abs(α) = e^{h(α)} (NumberField.absMulHeight₁); for a rational x/y in lowest terms H_abs = max(|x|, |y|) (Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max). Evertse's naive height H (DT.0/naive-height-of-algebraic-number) satisfies 2^{−d}H(α) ≤ H_abs(α)^d ≤ √(d+1)·H(α) for α of degree d (DT.0/height-comparisons). Proposed declaration: LogarithmicForms.yu.
hypotheses: α_j ∈ ℚ̄^×, K = ℚ(α)
𝔭 | p
α^b ≠ 1
proofSteps: Proved in Yu's papers (Compositio 74 (1990), 91 (1994)), not decomposed here: see the gap 'Proofs of the quantitative linear-form bounds'. Yu's proof passes to p-adic logarithms internally: for α with ord_𝔭 α = 0, not a root of unity, and s least with α^s ≡ 1 mod 𝔭, one has ord_p(α^{sp^κ} − 1) > 1/(p − 1) (Yu 1990, (1.6)-(1.8)), where the p-adic exponential and logarithm are inverse, so ord_p(α^b − 1) ≤ ord_p(α^{bsp^κ} − 1) = ord_p(b·log(α^{sp^κ})) (Yu 1990, Lemma 1.4).
acceptance: The dependence on p is through p^{f_𝔭} − 1 ≤ p^d − 1 and (log p)^{−(n+1)}; ED.2 needs exactly this explicit dependence.
Sharper bounds (Yu 2007, Forum Math.) are publicly restated by Gherga-Siksek, arXiv:2207.14492, Theorem 5.4; the 1994 statement is the one read in the primary source.

nodes.title: Lifting the exponent: |(1 + a)^b − 1|_p = |ab|_p (Evertse Exercise 5.9(i))
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and a ≠ 0 an integer with p | a if p is odd and 4 | a if p = 2. Then for every integer b ≥ 1: |(1 + a)^b − 1|_p = |ab|_p ≥ 1/|ab|; equivalently v_p((1 + a)^b − 1) = v_p(a) + v_p(b). Proposed declaration: LogarithmicForms.padicNorm_one_add_pow_sub_one.
hypotheses: p | a (p odd), 4 | a (p = 2)
proofSteps: p odd: Int.emultiplicity_pow_sub_pow with x = 1 + a, y = 1 (p | x − y = a, p ∤ x) gives v_p(x^b − 1) = v_p(a) + v_p(b).
p = 2: Int.two_pow_sub_pow' with 4 | x − y = a, 2 ∤ x.
For a nonzero integer N, |N|_p = p^{−v_p(N)} ≥ 1/|N| because p^{v_p(N)} divides N (padicNorm).

nodes.title: The case m = 1 of Yu's theorem for rationals, by elementary means
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and a ∈ ℚ^× with |a|_p = 1. There is c ∈ (0, 1], depending only on a and p, such that for every b ∈ ℤ with a^b ≠ 1: |a^b − 1|_p ≥ c·|b|_p ≥ c/|b|. Proposed declaration: LogarithmicForms.padicNorm_pow_sub_one_ge.
hypotheses: a^b ≠ 1
proofSteps: Write a = u/v with u, v ∈ ℤ prime to p; |a^b − 1|_p = |u^b − v^b|_p, and for b < 0 use a^b − 1 = −a^b(a^{−b} − 1) with |a^b|_p = 1.
Let t ≥ 1 be least with p | u^t − v^t (p odd; t | p − 1) or 4 | u^t − v^t (p = 2; t ≤ 2). If t ∤ b then p ∤ u^b − v^b and |a^b − 1|_p = 1.

If b = tb' then u^b − v^b = (u^t)^{b'} − (v^t)^{b'} and lifting the exponent (Int.emultiplicity_pow_sub_pow, Int.two_pow_sub_pow') gives |a^b − 1|_p = |a^t − 1|_p·|b'|_p ≥ |a^t − 1|_p·|b|_p; take c := min(1, |a^t − 1|_p) (and a^t ≠ 1 unless a = ±1, where the claim is checked directly).

a^b ≠ 1

nodes.title: The group U_S of rational S-units
nodes.statement: For a finite set S of natural numbers (in applications, of prime numbers), the group of rational S-units is the subgroup U_S := {x ∈ ℚ^× : v_p(x) = 0 for every prime p ∉ S} of ℚ^×, where v_p = padicValRat p. When every element of S is prime, U_S = {±∏_{p∈S} p^{z_p} : z ∈ ℤ^S} (Evertse §5.4), U_S ≅ {±1} × ℤ^S, and x ∈ U_S exactly when |num x| and den x are positive integers composed of primes of S (Nat.factoredNumbers S). The sign is part of U_S; −1 ∈ U_∅.
hypotheses: S : Finset ℕ; the defining condition is imposed only at primes outside S, so non-primes in S are harmless
Convention: U_S is a Subgroup of the unit group ℚ^× (Mathlib's ℚˣ), not a subset of ℚ
proofSteps: Carrier {x : ℚˣ | ∀ p prime, p ∉ S → padicValRat p x = 0}; closure under 1, products and inverses from padicValRat.mul and padicValRat.inv (valuations of nonzero rationals are additive).
Characterisation by numerator and denominator: v_p(x) = v_p(num) − v_p(den) with num and den coprime, so v_p(x) = 0 exactly when p divides neither.
Sign-times-product form: write x = sign(x)·∏_p p^{v_p(x)} (unique factorisation of num and den, Nat.factorization_prod_pow_eq_self).

Compatibility with Mathlib: under Rat.HeightOneSpectrum.primesEquiv the height-one primes of 𝓞 ℚ correspond to rational primes, and the valuation at the prime ideal (p) is exp(−v_p); hence U_S = Set.unit S' ℚ for S' the image of S.
acceptance: U_{2,3,5} contains 12/5 and −15/8 but not 7.
ratSUnits_mono and ratSUnits_mulEquiv agree on S ⊆ T: the inclusion U_S → U_T is (±1, z) ↦ (±1, z extended by 0).

nodes.title: Representatives of the divisors of an algebraic integer up to units
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d, r = rank K its unit rank, u : Fin r → (𝓞 K)^× a family of units, and put c₁(u) := r·Σ_j ‖L(u_j)‖_∞, where L = logEmbedding K (so L(x)_w = m_w log w(x) for the infinite places w ≠ w₀). For α ∈ 𝓞 K define D_u(α) := {γ ∈ 𝓞 K : γ ∣ α and house(γ) ≤ e^{c₁(u)} |N_{K/ℚ}(α)|^{1/d}}. When u has maximal rank and α ≠ 0 this is a finite set containing a unit multiple of every divisor of α (Evertse, Corollary 5.11).
hypotheses: The constant c₁(u) is explicit in the logarithmic embeddings of the u_j; for u = fundSystem K it depends only on K and the chosen fundamental units
|N_{K/ℚ}(α)|^{1/d} is the real d-th root of the absolute value of the rational number N(α)
Divisibility is in 𝓞 K
proofSteps: Set-builder definition; membership is definitional (mem_boundedDivisors).
Finiteness and the representation property are the separate nodes bounded-divisor-representatives-finite and divisors-up-to-units, which the Thue and Thue–Mahler reductions consume.
acceptance: For K = ℚ (rank 0, c₁ = 0, d = 1) D(m) is the set of divisors γ of m with |γ| ≤ |m|, i.e. all divisors.
D_u(ηα) = D_u(α) for every unit η (divisibility and |N| are unit-invariant).

nodes.title: Solving x ≤ a + b log x explicitly
nodes.statement: Let a ∈ ℝ, b > 0 and x > 0 with x ≤ a + b·log x. Then x ≤ 2a + 2b(log(2b) − 1). In particular, if a = b > 0 then x ≤ 2b·log(2b).
hypotheses: b > 0 and x > 0; a is arbitrary (it may be negative)
proofSteps: For c > 0 and x > 0: log x = log(x/c) + log c ≤ x/c − 1 + log c (Real.log_le_sub_one_of_pos applied to x/c).
Take c = 2b: b·log x ≤ x/2 − b + b·log(2b).
Substitute into x ≤ a + b·log x to get x/2 ≤ a − b + b·log(2b), i.e. x ≤ 2a + 2b(log(2b) − 1).
acceptance: a = 0, b = 10: the largest solution of x = 10 log x is ≈ 35.77, and the bound 20(log 20 − 1) ≈ 39.9 exceeds it.
a = b = C/log 2 is the form used for the S-unit equation (Theorem 5.17), giving B ≤ (2C/log 2)·log(2C/log 2).

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Theorem 5.12, printed p. 95

nodes.title: Conjugate algebraic numbers have the same degree, height and Mahler measure
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, α ∈ K and σ : K →+* ℂ. Then minpoly_ℚ(σ(α)) = minpoly_ℚ(α). Consequently deg σ(α) = deg α, H(σ(α)) = H(α) for the naive height of DT.0 (the maximum of the coefficients of the primitive minimal polynomial) and M(σ(α)) = M(α). Hence every constant that depends only on the degrees and heights of α_1, …, α_m (as in Evertse's Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3, Theorem 5.4) takes the same value for (σ(α_1), …, σ(α_m)).
hypotheses: σ is a ring homomorphism K → ℂ, viewed as a ℚ-algebra homomorphism (RingHom.toRatAlgHom); it is injective because K is a field
proofSteps: minpoly.algHom_eq applied to σ.toRatAlgHom (injective) gives equality of minimal polynomials over ℚ.
The primitive minimal polynomial and the Mahler measure are functions of the minimal polynomial (DT.0 definitions), so they coincide.
acceptance: For α = √2 ∈ ℚ(√2) and σ(√2) = −√2: both have minimal polynomial X² − 2, degree 2 and H = 2.
Used to make the constant C′ in the proof of Theorem 5.12 independent of the embedding σ_i.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Theorem 5.12, printed p. 95
sources.excerpt: So we can apply Corollary 5.3 and obtain |Λi| ⩾ (eB)^{−C′} for some effectively computable number C′ depending on α, ε1, . . . , εr and the finitely many roots of unity of K.
sources.match: The source's C′ is applied to the conjugates σ_i(α), σ_i(ε_j) but stated in terms of α, ε_j; this lemma is the degree/height conversion that justifies it.

nodes.title: Conjugates of a unit are controlled by its house
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and u ∈ (𝓞 K)^×. Then house(u) ≥ 1 and, for every embedding σ : K →+* ℂ, house(u)^{−(d−1)} ≤ |σ(u)| ≤ house(u); hence |log|σ(u)|| ≤ (d − 1)·log house(u).
hypotheses: u is a unit of the ring of integers, so |N_{K/ℚ}(u)| = 1
proofSteps: house(u) ≥ 1: NumberField.one_le_house_of_isIntegral (u ≠ 0 is integral).
Upper bound |σ(u)| ≤ house(u): NumberField.norm_embedding_le_house.
Lower bound: NumberField.norm_norm_le_norm_mul_house_pow gives |N(u)| ≤ |σ(u)|·house(u)^{d−1}, and |N(u)| = 1 (NumberField.Units.norm).
Take logarithms; log house(u) ≥ 0.
acceptance: K = ℚ(√2), u = 1 + √2: house = 1 + √2, the other conjugate has absolute value (1 + √2)^{−1} = house^{−(d−1)}, equality.
Evertse states the weaker |log|σ_j(ε)|| ≤ d·log house(ε); the factor d − 1 is what the product formula gives.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Lemma 5.9, printed p. 92
sources.excerpt: By Lemma 3.6 from Chapter 3 we have ⌈ε⌉ ⩾ 1 and by exercise 3.7 (i) from Chapter 3 we have |σj(ε)| ⩾ ⌈ε⌉^{1−d} for j = 1, . . . , d. Hence |log |σj(ε)|| ⩽ d log ⌈ε⌉ for j = 1, . . . , d.
sources.match: The same inequalities, with the sharper factor d − 1; Lemma 3.6 and Exercise 3.7(i) are replaced by the Mathlib house lemmas.

nodes.title: A unit has a conjugate at most house^{−1/(d−1)}
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d ≥ 2 and y ∈ (𝓞 K)^×. There is an embedding σ : K →+* ℂ with |σ(y)| ≤ house(y)^{−1/(d−1)}.
hypotheses: d ≥ 2 (for K = ℚ the statement is meaningless and the unit group is {±1})
proofSteps: ∏_σ |σ(y)| = |N_{K/ℚ}(y)| = 1 (Algebra.norm_eq_prod_embeddings, NumberField.Units.norm).

Let σ₀ attain house(y) (NumberField.house_eq_sup') and σ₁ minimise |σ(y)|; the d − 1 factors other than σ₀ are each ≥ |σ₁(y)|, so 1 ≥ house(y)·|σ₁(y)|^{d−1} (NumberField.Embeddings.card: there are d embeddings).
Rearrange.
acceptance: K = ℚ(√2), y = (1 + √2)^n: the small conjugate is (1 + √2)^{−n} = house^{−1}.
The bound is used with house(y) ≥ e^{B/κ} to make |σ(y)| exponentially small in the exponent size B.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Theorem 5.12, printed p. 95
sources.excerpt: In fact, let |σi(y)| be the smallest, and |σj(y)| = ⌈y⌉ the largest among |σ1(y)|, . . . , |σd(y)|. Then by Lemma 5.7, |σi(y)|^{d−1} · ⌈y⌉ ⩽ 1.
sources.match: Exactly this step.

nodes.title: Exponents of a unit are bounded by the logarithm of its house (Lemma 5.9)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d, r = rank K, and u : Fin r → (𝓞 K)^× a family of maximal rank (IsMaxRank u: the vectors L(u_j) = logEmbedding(u_j) are ℝ-linearly independent). Let T_u : logSpace K → ℝ^r be the coordinate map of the basis basisOfIsMaxRank u and κ(u) := ‖T_u‖ its operator norm for the sup norms (equal to the maximal absolute row sum of the inverse of the r×r matrix (m_w log w(u_j))). If x ∈ (𝓞 K)^×, ζ ∈ torsion K and e ∈ ℤ^r satisfy x = ζ·∏_j u_j^{e_j}, then |e_j| ≤ 2(d − 1)·κ(u)·log house(x) for every j.
hypotheses: u has maximal rank; it need not be a fundamental system (for u = fundSystem K every unit has such a representation, by NumberField.Units.exist_unique_eq_mul_prod)
The bound concerns every representation x = ζ∏u_j^{e_j}; for a maximal-rank family the exponent vector is determined by x
proofSteps: L is a homomorphism killing torsion (logEmbedding_eq_zero_iff), so L(x) = Σ_j e_j L(u_j) = Σ_j e_j·(basisOfIsMaxRank u)_j, hence e = T_u(L(x)).
|e_j| ≤ ‖T_u(L(x))‖_∞ ≤ κ(u)·‖L(x)‖_∞ (ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm).
‖L(x)‖_∞ = max_{w≠w₀} m_w|log w(x)| ≤ 2(d − 1)·log house(x) by unit-conjugate-log-bound (w(x) = |σ_w(x)|, m_w ≤ 2).
acceptance: K = ℚ(√2), u = (1 + √2): r = 1, κ = 1/log(1 + √2) and the bound for x = u^n reads |n| ≤ 2|n|.
The constant is explicit: an explicit fundamental system (as certified in tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/NumberFieldArithmetic layer 7.4) yields an explicit κ.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 5.9. There is an effectively computable number C > 0 depending on K, ε1, . . . , εr, such that for every ε ∈ O∗K we have max(|b1|, . . . , |br|) ⩽ C · log ⌈ε⌉, where b1, . . . , br are the integers defined by (5.1).
sources.match: Lemma 5.9 with C = 2(d−1)κ(u); the source inverts an r×r submatrix of the log matrix, which is the coordinate map T_u here.

nodes.title: Covering radius of the unit lattice
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and u : Fin r → (𝓞 K)^× of maximal rank. For every v ∈ logSpace K there is n ∈ ℤ^r with ‖v − L(∏_j u_j^{n_j})‖_∞ ≤ Σ_j ‖L(u_j)‖_∞.
hypotheses: u of maximal rank, so L(u_1), …, L(u_r) is an ℝ-basis b of logSpace K
proofSteps: Let b = basisOfIsMaxRank u. ZSpan.fract b v = v − ZSpan.floor b v (ZSpan.fract_apply) and ZSpan.floor b v = Σ_j ⌊b.repr v j⌋·b_j = L(∏ u_j^{⌊·⌋}).
ZSpan.norm_fract_le: ‖ZSpan.fract b v‖ ≤ Σ_j ‖b_j‖.
acceptance: K = ℚ(√2): every real v lies within |log(1 + √2)| of a multiple of log(1 + √2).
The bound is explicit in the basis; the source's covering constant c(L) is this sum.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Lemma 5.10, printed p. 93
sources.excerpt: In general, if L is a lattice in H, then for every point x ∈ H there is a point u ∈ L such that ∥u − x∥2 ⩽ c(L) for some number c(L) depending only on L. This c(L) can be computed in terms of a basis of L.
sources.match: The covering statement with the explicit c(L) = Σ‖b_j‖ (sup norm instead of Euclidean norm).

nodes.title: Every nonzero integer has a balanced unit multiple (Lemma 5.10)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d, u : Fin r → (𝓞 K)^× of maximal rank and c₁(u) := r·Σ_j ‖L(u_j)‖_∞. For every nonzero α ∈ 𝓞 K there is ε = ∏_j u_j^{n_j} such that |log w(εα) − (1/d)·log|N_{K/ℚ}(α)|| ≤ c₁(u) for every infinite place w. Consequently e^{−c₁}|N(α)|^{1/d} ≤ |σ(εα)| ≤ e^{c₁}|N(α)|^{1/d} for every embedding σ, and in particular house(εα) ≤ e^{c₁(u)}|N(α)|^{1/d}.
hypotheses: α ≠ 0 in 𝓞 K; u of maximal rank (ε lies in the subgroup generated by u)
For r = 0 the statement holds with c₁ = 0 (a single infinite place w with m_w = d and d·log w(α) = log|N(α)|)
proofSteps: Put t_w := log w(α) − (1/d)log|N(α)|. Then Σ_w m_w t_w = 0 (NumberField.InfinitePlace.prod_eq_abs_norm and NumberField.InfinitePlace.sum_mult_eq: Σ m_w = d).
Let v ∈ logSpace K with v_w = −m_w t_w (w ≠ w₀) and choose ε = ∏u_j^{n_j} by unit-lattice-covering-bound, so |L(ε)_w − v_w| ≤ R := Σ_j‖L(u_j)‖ for w ≠ w₀.
For w ≠ w₀: |log w(εα) − (1/d)log|N(α)|| = |log w(ε) + t_w| = |L(ε)_w − v_w|/m_w ≤ R.
For w₀: Σ_w m_w log w(ε) = 0 (NumberField.Units.sum_mult_mul_log) gives m_{w₀}(log w₀(ε) + t_{w₀}) = −Σ_{w≠w₀}(L(ε)_w − v_w), of absolute value ≤ rR; divide by m_{w₀} ≥ 1.
Exponentiate; house(εα) = max_σ |σ(εα)| = max_w w(εα) (NumberField.InfinitePlace.norm_embedding_eq).
acceptance: K = ℚ(√2), α = 7 + 5√2 = (1 + √2)³ is a unit; ε = α^{−1} gives εα = 1 and the bound reads 1 ≤ e^{c₁}.
For K = ℚ the lemma is the identity |α| = |N(α)|.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, Lemma 5.10 and proof, printed pp. 92-93
sources.excerpt: Lemma 5.10. There is an effectively computable number c > 1 with the following property: for every non-zero α ∈ OK there is ε ∈ O∗K such that (5.2) c^{−1}|NK/Q(α)|^{1/d} ⩽ ⌈εα⌉ ⩽ c|NK/Q(α)|^{1/d}.
sources.match: Lemma 5.10 with c = e^{c₁(u)}, and the place-by-place form the source's proof establishes.

nodes.title: The divisor representatives form a finite set
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, u : Fin r → (𝓞 K)^× and α ∈ 𝓞 K nonzero. Then D_u(α) (bounded-divisor-representatives) is finite.
hypotheses: α ≠ 0 (for α = 0 every γ divides α and the bound is 0 only when r = 0; the set is not claimed finite)
proofSteps: D_u(α) ⊆ {γ ∈ 𝓞 K : ∀σ, |σ(γ)| ≤ e^{c₁}|N(α)|^{1/d}} (NumberField.norm_embedding_le_house).
The image of the latter in K is {x ∈ K : x integral, ∀σ |σ(x)| ≤ B}, finite by NumberField.Embeddings.finite_of_norm_le; the coercion 𝓞 K → K is injective.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, D(m) is the finite set of divisors of m.
The finite set is effectively enumerable: minimal polynomials of its elements have coefficients bounded by NumberField.Embeddings.coeff_bdd_of_norm_le (ED.2 performs the enumeration).

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Corollary 5.11, printed pp. 93-94
sources.excerpt: This implies that there are at most finitely many γ ∈ OK with ⌈γ⌉ ⩽ c|NK/Q(α)|^{1/d}. Using constructive algebraic number theory, we can effectively determine these, and check for each of these γ whether it divides α in OK.
sources.match: Finiteness of the candidate set; its enumeration is the constructive step the source delegates to constructive algebraic number theory.

nodes.title: Divisors of an algebraic integer up to units (Corollary 5.11)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, u : Fin r → (𝓞 K)^× of maximal rank and α ∈ 𝓞 K nonzero. For every β ∈ 𝓞 K with β ∣ α there are γ ∈ D_u(α) and ε ∈ (𝓞 K)^× with β = εγ.
hypotheses: u of maximal rank; β divides α in 𝓞 K
proofSteps: β ≠ 0 and |N(β)| ≤ |N(α)|: N is multiplicative and N(α/β) is a nonzero integer (Algebra.norm_eq_prod_embeddings / RingOfIntegers norm integrality).
balanced-unit-multiple applied to β gives ε' with house(ε'β) ≤ e^{c₁}|N(β)|^{1/d} ≤ e^{c₁}|N(α)|^{1/d}.
γ := ε'β divides α (unit multiple of a divisor), so γ ∈ D_u(α) and β = ε'^{−1}γ.
acceptance: K = ℚ: every divisor of m is ±γ with γ a positive divisor.
K = ℚ(i), α = 5: the divisors 2 ± i and their unit multiples are represented by elements of house ≤ √5·e^{0} (rank 0).

sources.excerpt: Corollary 5.11. Given α ∈ OK \ {0}, one can effectively determine a finite set of divisors γ1, . . . , γm of α in OK such that for each divisor β of α in OK there are ε ∈ O∗K and i ∈ {1, . . . , m} such that β = εγi.
sources.match: Corollary 5.11 with the explicit finite set D_u(α).

nodes.title: Exponent of a prime in an integer versus its logarithm
nodes.statement: For a prime p and a positive integer n: v_p(n)·log p ≤ log n. Consequently, for x ∈ U_S written x = u/w in lowest terms, |v_p(x)|·log p ≤ log max(|u|, w) = log H(x) for every prime p, and |v_p(x)| ≤ log H(x)/log 2.
hypotheses: n ≠ 0; H(x) = Height.mulHeight₁ x = max(|num x|, den x) (Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max)
proofSteps: p^{v_p(n)} ∣ n (pow_padicValNat_dvd), hence p^{v_p(n)} ≤ n and take logarithms.
For x = u/w coprime, v_p(x) is v_p(|u|) or −v_p(w), and both |u|, w ≤ H(x).
acceptance: For Tijdeman's theorem the bound gives max_p|v_p(x) − v_p(y)| ≤ log y/log 2 for S-integers x < y.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Theorem 5.6, printed p. 89
sources.excerpt: Note that ki ⩽ log an / log pi ⩽ log an / log 2, li ⩽ log an−1 / log pi ⩽ log an / log 2 for i = 1, . . . , t, hence B ⩽ log an/ log 2.
sources.match: The exponent–height conversion used in Theorems 5.6 and 5.17.

nodes.title: Lower bound for |a^m − b^n| (Corollary 5.5, first part)
nodes.statement: Let a, b ≥ 2 be integers and C₁ > 0 such that for all integers k, l with b^k a^{−l} ≠ 1: |b^k a^{−l} − 1| ≥ (e·max(1, |k|, |l|))^{−C₁} (this is Corollary 5.3, or Theorem 5.4, for the pair (b, a)). Then for all positive integers m, n with a^m ≠ b^n: |a^m − b^n| ≥ max(a^m, b^n)·(e·max(m, n))^{−C₁}.
hypotheses: The hypothesis is the multiplicative lower bound for the linear form in log b and log a with integer exponents of either sign
a^m ≠ b^n (the bound says nothing when the linear form vanishes)
proofSteps: If a^m > b^n: |a^m − b^n| = a^m·|1 − b^n a^{−m}| and apply the hypothesis with (k, l) = (n, m); max(1, n, m) = max(m, n).
If b^n > a^m: |a^m − b^n| = b^n·|a^m b^{−n} − 1| and a^m b^{−n} = b^{−n}a^{−(−m)}; apply the hypothesis with (k, l) = (−n, −m).
acceptance: (a, b) = (3, 2), (m, n) = (2, 3): |9 − 8| = 1 ≥ 9·(3e)^{−C₁} forces C₁ ≥ log 9/log(3e) ≈ 1.0; any valid C₁ passes.
The inequality is homogeneous in the size of a^m, which is what makes it useful for a^m − b^n = k.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, Corollary 5.5 and proof, printed p. 88
sources.excerpt: Then there is an effectively computable number C1 > 0, depending only on a, b, such that for any two positive integers m, n with a^m ≠ b^n, |a^m − b^n| ⩾ max(a^m, b^n)/(e max(m, n))^{C1}.
sources.match: First assertion of Corollary 5.5 in transfer form (C₁ is the hypothesis).

nodes.title: Explicit bound for a^m − b^n = k in terms of the logarithmic-form constant
nodes.statement: Let a, b ≥ 2, k ≠ 0 be integers and C₁ > 0 as in pillai-difference-lower-bound. Every pair of positive integers (m, n) with a^m − b^n = k satisfies max(m, n) ≤ 2(log|k| + C₁)/log 2 + 2(C₁/log 2)(log(2C₁/log 2) − 1).
hypotheses: k ≠ 0, so a^m ≠ b^n
proofSteps: B := max(m, n); max(a^m, b^n) ≥ 2^B.
pillai-difference-lower-bound: |k| ≥ 2^B (eB)^{−C₁}, i.e. B·log 2 ≤ log|k| + C₁ + C₁·log B.
log-linear-inequality-bound with a' = (log|k| + C₁)/log 2 and b' = C₁/log 2.
acceptance: 3^m − 2^n = 1 has the solutions (1, 1) and (2, 3); both satisfy the bound for every admissible C₁.
2^m − 3^n = 5 has the solutions (3, 1) and (5, 3); the bound must dominate 5.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, Corollary 5.5 and proof, printed p. 88
sources.excerpt: Consequently, for any non-zero integer k, there exists an effectively computable number C2, depending on a, b, k such that if m, n are positive integers with a^m − b^n = k, then m, n ⩽ C2.
sources.match: Second assertion of Corollary 5.5 with C₂ explicit in C₁ and k.

nodes.title: Effective finiteness for a^m − b^n = k with Matveev's constant
nodes.statement: For integers a, b ≥ 2 and k ≠ 0 the set {(m, n) ∈ ℤ_{>0}² : a^m − b^n = k} is finite, and each element satisfies max(m, n) ≤ 2(log|k| + C₁)/log 2 + 2(C₁/log 2)(log(2C₁/log 2) − 1) with C₁ = (e/2)·2^{4.5}·30^5·max(1, log a)·max(1, log b), Matveev's constant (Evertse, Theorem 5.4, with m = 2 and H(a) = a, H(b) = b).
hypotheses: a, b ≥ 2 integers; k ≠ 0
Theorem 5.4 is applied to the rationals (b, a) and integer exponents (k, −l) with b^k a^{−l} ≠ 1; B = max(|k|, |l|) ≥ 1 there, so max(1, |k|, |l|) = B
proofSteps: Theorem 5.4 (DT.3 matveev-explicit-lower-bound) supplies the hypothesis of pillai-difference-lower-bound with the stated C₁.
pillai-equation-exponent-bound gives the explicit bound on max(m, n); finiteness follows since m, n range over a bounded set of positive integers.
acceptance: For (a, b, k) = (3, 2, 1) the solution set is {(1, 1), (2, 3)}; ED.2's certified enumeration inside the box must return exactly these.
The same bound with C₁ from Corollary 5.3 (DT.3 baker-lower-bounds-for-linear-forms-in-logarithms) is Evertse's Corollary 5.5.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, Theorem 5.4 and Corollary 5.5, printed pp. 87-88
sources.excerpt: Proof. Let m, n be positive integers. Put B := max(m, n). Assume without loss of generality that a^m > b^n. By Corollary 5.3 or Theorem 5.4 we have |1 − b^n a^{−m}| ⩾ (eB)^{−C1}, where C1 is an effectively computable number depending only on a, b.
sources.match: Corollary 5.5 with Theorem 5.4 as the input, which makes C₁ numerical.

nodes.title: Gaps between S-integers in terms of the logarithmic-form constant
nodes.statement: Let S be a finite set of primes and C > 0 such that for every b ∈ ℤ^S with ∏_{p∈S} p^{b_p} ≠ 1: |∏_{p∈S} p^{b_p} − 1| ≥ (e·max_p|b_p|)^{−C} (Corollary 5.3 for the primes of S). Then for all positive integers x < y composed of primes of S (Nat.factoredNumbers S): y − x ≥ y·(e·log y/log 2)^{−C}.
hypotheses: x < y, both S-smooth (y ≥ 2 since y > x ≥ 1)
proofSteps: B ≤ max_p max(v_p(x), v_p(y)) ≤ log y/log 2 by prime-power-exponent-height-bound.
y − x = y·|x/y − 1| ≥ y(eB)^{−C} ≥ y(e·log y/log 2)^{−C} (monotonicity in B).
acceptance: S = {2, 3}, (x, y) = (8, 9): 1 ≥ 9(e·log 9/log 2)^{−C} holds for every admissible C (it forces C ≥ log 9/log(e·log 9/log 2) ≈ 1.0).
Exercise 5.3 (x and y from disjoint prime sets) is proved by the same argument.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Theorem 5.6, printed p. 89

nodes.title: Tijdeman's theorem on gaps between S-integers (Theorem 5.6)
nodes.statement: Let S = {p₁, …, p_t} be a finite set of primes and a₀ < a₁ < a₂ < … the positive integers composed of primes of S. There are effectively computable c₁, c₂ > 0, depending only on S, with a_n − a_{n−1} ≥ a_n/(c₁(log a_n)^{c₂}) for all n ≥ 1; one may take c₂ = C and c₁ = (e/log 2)^C with C the Corollary 5.3 constant for (p₁, …, p_t). More generally y − x ≥ y/(c₁(log y)^{c₂}) for all S-integers x < y.
hypotheses: S finite, all elements prime; a₀ = 1
n ≥ 1, so a_n ≥ 2 and log a_n > 0
proofSteps: Corollary 5.3 (DT.3) for the tuple (p₁, …, p_t) (none is 0 or 1) gives C.
gaps-between-s-integers-lower-bound with x = a_{n−1}, y = a_n; rewrite y(e log y/log 2)^{−C} = y/((e/log 2)^C (log y)^C).
acceptance: S = {2}: a_n = 2^n and a_n − a_{n−1} = a_n/2, consistent with any c₁ ≥ 2 (log a_n)^{−c₂}.
S = {2, 3}: the gap 9 − 8 = 1 at a_n = 9 must satisfy the inequality.

nodes.title: Explicit exponent bound for the unit equation in terms of the logarithmic-form constant
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d with unit rank r ≥ 1, u : Fin r → (𝓞 K)^× of maximal rank, α, β ∈ K^×, and C′ > 0 such that for every embedding σ : K →+* ℂ, every γ ∈ {αζ, βζ : ζ ∈ torsion K} and every e ∈ ℤ^r with σ(γ∏_j u_j^{e_j}) ≠ 1: |σ(γ∏_j u_j^{e_j}) − 1| ≥ (e·max(1, max_j|e_j|))^{−C′}. Put κ := 2(d − 1)κ(u) (unit-exponent-house-bound), H := max(house α, house β), A := κ(d − 1)(log H + C′) and B₀ := κ(d − 1)C′. If x, y ∈ (𝓞 K)^× satisfy αx + βy = 1 and x = ζ_x∏u_j^{e_j}, y = ζ_y∏u_j^{f_j} with ζ_x, ζ_y ∈ torsion K, then max_j max(|e_j|, |f_j|) ≤ max(1, 2A + 2B₀(log(2B₀) − 1)).
hypotheses: r ≥ 1 (hence d ≥ 2); the case r = 0 is handled in the theorem node, where the unit group is finite
The hypothesis is Corollary 5.3 in multiplicative form for the tuples (σ(γ), σ(u_1), …, σ(u_r)); it covers both α and β because the argument is applied to whichever of x, y has the larger exponents
proofSteps: Let B be the maximum; assume B ≥ 1 and, by symmetry (swap (x, α) and (y, β)), that B = max_j|f_j| ≥ max_j|e_j|.
unit-exponent-house-bound: B ≤ κ·log house(y), so house(y) ≥ e^{B/κ}.
small-conjugate-of-unit: some σ has |σ(y)| ≤ house(y)^{−1/(d−1)} ≤ e^{−B/(κ(d−1))}.
Λ := |σ(αx) − 1| = |σ(βy)| ≤ house(β)·e^{−B/(κ(d−1))} (NumberField.norm_embedding_le_house) and Λ ≠ 0 since βy ≠ 0.
αx = (αζ_x)∏u_j^{e_j} with max(1, max|e_j|) ≤ B, so the hypothesis gives Λ ≥ (eB)^{−C′}.
Hence B ≤ κ(d−1)(log house β + C′) + κ(d−1)C′·log B ≤ A + B₀·log B; conclude with log-linear-inequality-bound.
acceptance: The bound is monotone in C′, κ and H, so any valid C′ from DT.3 may be used.

K = ℚ(√2), α = β = 1: x + y = 1 has no solution in units, since for units a + b√2 and (1 − a) − b√2 the norms a² − 2b² and (1 − a)² − 2b² ∈ {±1} would differ by the odd number 1 − 2a; the bound is vacuous but the hypotheses must still be checkable.

nodes.title: Effective finiteness of the unit equation (Theorem 5.12)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and α, β ∈ K^×. The set of (x, y) ∈ (𝓞 K)^× × (𝓞 K)^× with αx + βy = 1 is finite. Effectively: if rank K = 0 the unit group is the finite group torsion K; if rank K ≥ 1, let u = fundSystem K and C′ the maximum of the Corollary 5.3 constants for the finitely many tuples (γ, u_1, …, u_r) and (u_1, …, u_r), γ ∈ {αζ, βζ : ζ ∈ torsion K}, γ ≠ 1; then every solution has exponent vectors (with respect to u) bounded by the bound of unit-equation-exponent-bound, so the solutions lie in the explicit finite region {ζ∏u_j^{e_j} : ζ ∈ torsion K, max|e_j| ≤ B}².
hypotheses: α, β ≠ 0
Corollary 5.3 needs its algebraic numbers ≠ 0, 1: the fundamental units are not roots of unity, and a factor σ(γ) = 1 is dropped from the tuple
Effectivity refers to the explicit dependence of the region on C′, d, κ(u) and the houses of α, β; the enumeration of the region is EffectiveDiophantineMethods:ED.2
proofSteps: rank K = 0: (𝓞 K)^× = torsion K is finite (NumberField.Units.exist_unique_eq_mul_prod with Fin 0), so the solution set is finite.
rank K ≥ 1: fundSystem K has maximal rank (NumberField.Units.isMaxRank_fundSystem) and every unit is ζ∏u_j^{e_j} (NumberField.Units.exist_unique_eq_mul_prod).

For each σ and γ apply Corollary 5.3 (DT.3) to (σ(γ), σ(u_1), …, σ(u_r)) with exponents (1, e); by conjugate-invariance-of-degree-and-height its constant does not depend on σ; torsion K is finite, so C′ is a maximum over finitely many tuples.
unit-equation-exponent-bound bounds every exponent by B; finitely many (ζ, e) with max|e_j| ≤ B, hence finitely many solutions.
acceptance: Every unit equation over an imaginary quadratic field has at most (#torsion K)² solutions.
K = ℚ(cos(2π/19)), degree 9, rank 8, x + y = 1: Wildanger (2000) determined all solutions; ED.2's enumeration within this region must reproduce his list.
Special case of gyory-effective-finiteness with Γ = (𝓞 K)^×.

nodes.title: Siegel's identity
nodes.statement: In every commutative ring, (α₂ − α₃)(X − α₁Y) + (α₃ − α₁)(X − α₂Y) + (α₁ − α₂)(X − α₃Y) = 0. Consequently, in a field, if α₁, α₂, α₃ are pairwise distinct and X − α₃Y ≠ 0, then ((α₂ − α₃)/(α₂ − α₁))·(X − α₁Y)/(X − α₃Y) + ((α₃ − α₁)/(α₂ − α₁))·(X − α₂Y)/(X − α₃Y) = 1.
hypotheses: For the field form: α₁ ≠ α₂ and X − α₃Y ≠ 0
proofSteps: Expand (ring).
Move the third term to the right-hand side as (α₂ − α₁)(X − α₃Y) and divide by it.
acceptance: This is the identity (5.6) of Evertse that turns a Thue equation into a unit equation.

sources.locator: Chapter 5, proof of Theorem 5.13, printed p. 97

nodes.title: Reduction of a Thue equation to a monic form
nodes.statement: Let f ∈ ℤ[X] have degree d ≥ 1 and leading coefficient a₀, F := f.homogenize d (the binary form Σ a_i X^{d−i}Y^i with F(X, 1) = f), g := integralNormalization f (the monic polynomial a₀^{d−1}f(X/a₀)) and G := g.homogenize d. For all x, y, m ∈ ℤ: F(x, y) = m ⟺ G(a₀x, y) = a₀^{d−1}m. Hence (x, y) ↦ (a₀x, y) is a bijection from the solutions of F(x, y) = m onto the solutions (x′, y′) of G(x′, y′) = a₀^{d−1}m with a₀ ∣ x′, and the complex zeros of g are a₀ times those of f (so g has as many distinct zeros as f).
hypotheses: deg f = d ≥ 1, so a₀ ≠ 0 is the coefficient of X^d in F
proofSteps: Coefficientwise: G = X^d + Σ_{i<d} coeff_i(f)·a₀^{d−1−i}X^iY^{d−i}; evaluate at (a₀x, y) and factor a₀^{d−1} (coeff_d(f) = a₀).
Zeros: integralNormalization_aeval_eq_zero sends a zero z of f to the zero a₀z of g; comparing degrees these are all zeros with multiplicity.
acceptance: F = 2X³ − Y³, m = 3: G = X³ − 4Y³ and F(x, y) = 3 ⟺ G(2x, y) = 12.
Solution sets correspond exactly (no solution is lost or added): the acceptance condition of DT.4.

nodes.title: Factorisation of a monic binary form over a splitting field
nodes.statement: Let g ∈ ℤ[X] be monic of degree d and K a number field with g = ∏_{i=1}^{d}(X − θ_i) in 𝓞 K[X] (roots listed with multiplicity; roots of a monic integer polynomial are algebraic integers). Then for all x, y ∈ ℤ: G(x, y) = ∏_i (x − θ_i y) in 𝓞 K, where G = g.homogenize d. Consequently, if G(x, y) = m ≠ 0 then every x − θ_i y is a nonzero divisor of m in 𝓞 K and |N_{K/ℚ}(x − θ_i y)| ≤ |m|^{[K:ℚ]}.
hypotheses: g monic and split over K (e.g. K the splitting field, Polynomial.SplittingField)
proofSteps: homogenize is multiplicative for polynomials of the right degrees (Polynomial.homogenize_finsetProd) and homogenize (X − C θ) 1 = X₀ − θX₁.
Evaluate at (x, y); divisibility is immediate from the product; |N| is multiplicative and |N(m)| = |m|^{[K:ℚ]}.

nodes.title: A Thue equation reduces to finitely many unit equations
nodes.statement: Let g ∈ ℤ[X] be monic with three distinct zeros θ₀, θ₁, θ₂ in 𝓞 K (K a number field, u = fundSystem K), m ≠ 0 and D := D_u(m) (bounded-divisor-representatives). For every (x, y) ∈ ℤ² with G(x, y) = m there are μ₀, μ₁, μ₂ ∈ D and units ε₀, ε₁, ε₂ with x − θ_i y = μ_i ε_i, and (X, Y) := (ε₀/ε₂, ε₁/ε₂) solves the unit equation a(μ)X + b(μ)Y = 1 with a(μ) = ((θ₁ − θ₂)/(θ₁ − θ₀))(μ₀/μ₂), b(μ) = ((θ₂ − θ₀)/(θ₁ − θ₀))(μ₁/μ₂). Conversely, when y ≠ 0, λ := (x − θ₀y)/(x − θ₂y) = (μ₀/μ₂)X determines x/y = (θ₀ − λθ₂)/(1 − λ).
hypotheses: θ₀, θ₁, θ₂ pairwise distinct zeros of g (Theorem 5.13 needs at least three distinct zeros)
m ≠ 0, so no factor x − θ_i y vanishes
proofSteps: thue-form-factorisation: each x − θ_i y divides m.
divisors-up-to-units: x − θ_i y = ε_i μ_i with μ_i ∈ D_u(m).
siegel-identity with (X, Y) = (x, y) and x − θ₂y ≠ 0 gives the unit equation for (ε₀/ε₂, ε₁/ε₂).
λ ≠ 1 because θ₀ ≠ θ₂ and y ≠ 0; solve x − θ₀y = λ(x − θ₂y) for x/y.
acceptance: g = X³ − 2 over K = ℚ(∛2, ω), m = 1: the solution (x, y) = (1, 0) gives μ_i = 1, ε_i = 1 and the unit equation solution (1, 1) with a + b = 1.
The reduction is solution-set preserving in the sense that (x, y) is recovered from (μ, X) (and the finitely many y = 0 solutions x^d = m are listed separately).

nodes.title: Height of a rational number computed in a number field
nodes.statement: For every number field K and q ∈ ℚ: Height.mulHeight₁ (q : K) = (Height.mulHeight₁ q)^{[K:ℚ]} = max(|num q|, den q)^{[K:ℚ]}; equivalently logHeight₁_K(q) = [K:ℚ]·log max(|num q|, den q).

proofSteps: mulHeight₁(a/b) = mulHeight ![a, b] (Height.mulHeight₁_div_eq_mulHeight) for coprime integers a, b.
NumberField.mulHeight_eq: infinite places contribute ∏_w max(|a|, |b|)^{m_w} = max(|a|, |b|)^{Σ m_w} = max(|a|,|b|)^{[K:ℚ]} (NumberField.InfinitePlace.sum_mult_eq).
Finite places: |a|_v, |b|_v ≤ 1 (NumberField.FinitePlace.norm_le_one) and 1 = sa + tb gives max(|a|_v, |b|_v) = 1.
Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max identifies the right-hand side.

q = 0: both sides equal 1.

nodes.statement: For a number field K of degree d and α ∈ 𝓞 K: logHeight₁(α) ≤ d·max(0, log house(α)).

Finite places contribute 0 (NumberField.FinitePlace.norm_le_one); w(α) ≤ house(α) (NumberField.norm_embedding_le_house) and Σ m_w = d.

nodes.title: Effective finiteness of Thue equations (Theorem 5.13)
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] be a binary form of degree d whose X^d-coefficient a₀ is nonzero and such that F(X, 1) has at least three distinct complex zeros, and let m ≠ 0. Then {(x, y) ∈ ℤ² : F(x, y) = m} is finite. Explicitly, with m′ := a₀^{d−1}m, g, G as in thue-equation-monic-reduction, θ₀, θ₁, θ₂ distinct zeros of g in the splitting field K of g (degree D), u = fundSystem K and B_T the maximum over (μ₀, μ₁, μ₂) ∈ D_u(m′)³ of the unit-equation exponent bound for (a(μ), b(μ)), every solution with y ≠ 0 satisfies log H(a₀x/y) ≤ h_T := 4·log⁺(e^{c₁(u)}|m′|) + 2B_T·Σ_j log house(u_j) + log⁺house(θ₀) + log⁺house(θ₂) + 2 log 2, and every solution satisfies max(|a₀x|, |y|) ≤ |m′|^{1/d}·e^{h_T}.
hypotheses: F(X, 1) = f has degree d (a₀ ≠ 0) and at least three distinct zeros; m ≠ 0
Each hypothesis is needed: x − 2y = 1 (degree 1), x² − 2y² = 1 (Pell, two zeros) and (x − y)³ = 1 (one distinct zero, solutions (t + 1, t)) all have infinitely many solutions
proofSteps: thue-equation-monic-reduction: pass to (x′, y′) = (a₀x, y) and G(x′, y′) = m′.

y′ ≠ 0: thue-equation-reduction-to-unit-equations gives μ ∈ D_u(m′)³ (finite by bounded-divisor-representatives-finite) and a solution of a(μ)X + b(μ)Y = 1 in units; effective-finiteness-for-unit-and-thue-equations bounds the exponents of X = ε₀/ε₂ by B_T.

Heights: λ = (μ₀/μ₂)X; Height.logHeight₁_mul_le, Height.logHeight₁_inv, Height.logHeight₁_zpow, Height.logHeight₁_prod_le and log-height-of-algebraic-integer-bound give logHeight₁(λ) ≤ 2D·log⁺(e^{c₁}|m′|) + B_T·D·Σ_j log house(u_j) (using house(μ_i) ≤ e^{c₁}|N(m′)|^{1/D} = e^{c₁}|m′|).
ξ := x′/y′ = (θ₀ − λθ₂)/(1 − λ): Height.logHeight₁_sub_le and Height.logHeight₁_add_le give logHeight₁(ξ) ≤ 2 logHeight₁(λ) + logHeight₁(θ₀) + logHeight₁(θ₂) + 2D log 2.
ξ ∈ ℚ: rational-height-in-number-field converts to log H(ξ) = logHeight₁_K(ξ)/D ≤ h_T.
Write ξ = p/q in lowest terms; (x′, y′) = k(p, q) and k^d G(p, q) = m′ with G(p, q) a nonzero integer, so |k| ≤ |m′|^{1/d} and max(|x′|, |y′|) ≤ |m′|^{1/d}H(ξ).
acceptance: x³ − 2y³ = 1 has exactly the solutions (1, 0) and (−1, −1); both lie in the box.
Hypothesis tests: x − 2y = 1, x² − 2y² = 1 and (x − y)³ = 1 have infinitely many solutions; when the X^d-coefficient vanishes the source reduces to y ∣ m instead.
ED.2's certified enumeration of the box for x³ − 2y³ = 1 must return exactly {(1, 0), (−1, −1)}.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 5.13. Let F ∈ Z[X, Y ] be a binary form of degree d. Suppose that the coefficient of X^d in F is non-zero and that F(X, 1) has at least three distinct zeros in C. Let m be a non-zero integer. Then the equation (5.5) F(x, y) = m in x, y ∈ Z has only finitely many solutions.

nodes.title: The equation y³ = 2x(x − 3) reduces to finitely many Thue equations
nodes.statement: Let A := {±2^k3^l : k, l ∈ {0, 1, 2}} (18 integers). For every (x, y) ∈ ℤ² with y³ = 2x(x − 3) there are a, b ∈ A and u, v ∈ ℤ with 2x = au³, x − 3 = bv³, and then au³ − 2bv³ = 6. Conversely, a solution (u, v) of au³ − 2bv³ = 6 with au³ even gives x := au³/2, and (x, y) solves y³ = 2x(x − 3) exactly when 2x(x − 3) is a cube. Hence the solution set of y³ = 2x(x − 3) is determined by the 324 Thue equations aU³ − 2bV³ = 6, each of which has finitely many solutions by thue-equation-effective-bound (aX³ − 2b has three distinct zeros).
hypotheses: The exponents k, l ∈ {0, 1, 2} absorb cubes of 2 and 3 into u, v
x = 0 and x = 3 (y = 0) are covered with u = 0 or v = 0
proofSteps: gcd(2x, x − 3) divides 2x − 2(x − 3) = 6.
For a prime p ≥ 5: p divides at most one of 2x, x − 3, and v_p(2x) + v_p(x − 3) = 3v_p(y), so each of v_p(2x), v_p(x − 3) is ≡ 0 mod 3 (when nonzero).
Write v_2 and v_3 of 2x and of x − 3 as 3s + k with k ∈ {0, 1, 2}; collect the cube parts into u³, v³ and the sign and the residual powers of 2, 3 into a, b ∈ A.
Each Thue form aU³ − 2bV³ has ab ≠ 0, so its dehomogenisation has three distinct zeros and thue-equation-effective-bound applies.
acceptance: The solutions x ∈ {0, 3, −1, 4, 12} (y ∈ {0, 0, 2, 2, 6}) arise: e.g. x = 4 gives 2x = 8 = 1·2³ and x − 3 = 1 = 1·1³, and 8 − 2 = 6.
The reduction loses no solution: every solution of y³ = 2x(x − 3) maps to a solution of one of the listed Thue equations (DT.4 acceptance).

sources.excerpt: The gcd of 2x and x−3 divides 6. So if p is a prime number ⩾ 5, then p divides at most one of 2x, x − 3 and if it divides one of these numbers, the exponent of p in the unique factorization of that number is divisible by 3.
sources.match: The reduction of (5.8) to the Thue equations au³ − 2bv³ = 6, stated as a solution-set correspondence.

nodes.title: Baker's theorem on superelliptic and hyperelliptic equations (Theorem 5.14)
nodes.statement: Let b ≠ 0 be an integer, n ≥ 2 and f ∈ ℤ[X] without multiple zeros, with deg f ≥ 2 if n ≥ 3 and deg f ≥ 3 if n = 2. Then b·y^n = f(x) has only finitely many solutions (x, y) ∈ ℤ², and they can be determined effectively. Explicitly (Bérczes–Evertse–Győry 2013, Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 with K = ℚ, S = {∞}, N := deg f, ĥ := log max(1, |b|, |coefficients of f|)): every solution satisfies log max(1, |x|), log max(1, |y|) ≤ (6N)^{14n³N³}·e^{8n²N³ĥ} if n ≥ 3, and ≤ (4N)^{212N⁴}·e^{50N⁴ĥ} if n = 2.
hypotheses: f separable over ℚ (no multiple zeros); the degree thresholds differ between n = 2 and n ≥ 3
The explicit bounds are those of the cited public source, specialised; Evertse states the theorem without proof
proofSteps: Proof route (Bérczes–Evertse–Győry, sections 3–5): factor f over its splitting field L; for a solution, the ideals (x − α_i) are, up to a finite set of ideals dividing a power of the discriminant and b, n-th powers; hence x − α_i = δ_i ξ_i^n with δ_i in an effectively determined finite set of L.

n ≥ 3: three such equations and Siegel's identity give a unit (S-unit) equation over L(δ^{1/n}); n = 2: pairs of equations give Thue equations of degree 2 over a larger field and a two-equation system; in both cases the S-unit bound (gyory-effective-finiteness, in the explicit Győry–Yu form) bounds the heights.
The worked example superelliptic-example-reduction is the case f = 2X(X − 3), n = 3, b = 1 over ℚ, where the reduction is to Thue equations over ℤ.

nodes.title: The Schinzel–Tijdeman theorem (Theorem 5.15)
nodes.statement: Let b ≠ 0 be an integer and f ∈ ℤ[X] of degree N ≥ 2 without multiple zeros. There is an effectively computable C, depending on f and b, such that if b·y^n = f(x) has a solution (x, y) ∈ ℤ² with y ∉ {0, ±1}, then n ≤ C. Explicitly (Bérczes–Evertse–Győry 2013, Theorem 2.3 with K = ℚ, S = {∞}): n ≤ (10N²)^{40N}·e^{11Nĥ}, ĥ = log max(1, |b|, |coefficients of f|).
hypotheses: y ∉ {0, ±1} (for those y every n works when f(x) ∈ {0, ±b} has a solution)
f separable of degree ≥ 2
proofSteps: Proof route (Schinzel–Tijdeman 1976; Bérczes–Evertse–Győry section 6): for large n a solution gives x − α_i = δ_i ξ_i^n with bounded δ_i; comparing two such equations produces a linear form in logarithms with the unknown exponent n as coefficient; Baker's lower bound (DT.3) against the upper bound |x|^{−…} forces n bounded.
acceptance: b = 1, f = X² + 7 (N = 2): y^n = x² + 7 with y = 2 has the solutions n = 3, 4, 5, 7, 15 (Ramanujan–Nagell: 2^{15} = 181² + 7); the bound must allow n = 15.
The conclusion is about n, not about x, y (for fixed n Theorem 5.14 applies).

nodes.title: Tijdeman's effective bound for Catalan's equation
nodes.statement: There is an effectively computable constant C such that every solution of x^m − y^n = 1 in integers x, y, m, n ≥ 2 satisfies x^m, y^n ≤ C.

nodes.title: The elementary p-adic bound for one logarithm (Exercise 5.9)
nodes.statement: Let p be prime and a ∈ ℤ nonzero with p ∣ a, and 4 ∣ a if p = 2. For every positive integer b: v_p((1 + a)^b − 1) = v_p(a) + v_p(b); equivalently |(1 + a)^b − 1|_p = |ab|_p ≥ 1/|ab|.

proofSteps: Lifting the exponent: for x ≡ y mod p (mod 4 if p = 2), p ∤ xy, v_p(x^b − y^b) = v_p(x − y) + v_p(b) (Int.emultiplicity_pow_sub_pow, padicValNat.pow_sub_pow); apply with x = 1 + a, y = 1.
|ab|_p = p^{−v_p(a) − v_p(b)} ≥ 1/|ab| since p^{v_p(a)} ≤ |a| and p^{v_p(b)} ≤ b.

nodes.title: The S-unit equation over ℚ as u + v = w in coprime S-integers
nodes.statement: Let S be a finite set of primes. For x, y ∈ U_S with x + y = 1 there are pairwise coprime integers u, v, w with w > 0, u + v = w, x = u/w, y = v/w, and |u|, |v|, w composed of primes of S. The map (x, y) ↦ (u, v, w) is a bijection from the solutions of x + y = 1 in U_S² onto such triples, and max_p max(|v_p(x)|, |v_p(y)|) = max_p max(v_p(u), v_p(v), v_p(w)); each prime divides at most one of u, v, w.
hypotheses: S consists of primes
w > 0 normalises the sign
proofSteps: w := lcm(den x, den y) > 0, u := xw, v := yw are integers with u + v = w; gcd(u, v, w) = 1 by minimality of w.
Pairwise coprimality: a prime dividing two of u, v, w divides the third (u + v = w), contradicting gcd = 1.
A prime p ∣ u has v_p(x) = v_p(u) > 0 (p ∤ w), so p ∈ S; similarly for v, w (v_p(x) = −v_p(w) < 0).
The exponent identity follows since exactly one of u, v, w carries each prime; the inverse map is (u, v, w) ↦ (u/w, v/w).

nodes.title: Effective finiteness of the S-unit equation over ℚ (Theorem 5.17)
nodes.statement: For every finite set S of primes, x + y = 1 has only finitely many solutions (x, y) ∈ U_S × U_S, and every solution satisfies |v_p(x)|, |v_p(y)| ≤ max(1, (2C_S/log 2)log(2C_S/log 2)) for all p, where C_S is the maximum over p ∈ S of the Theorem 5.16 constants C(p; −1, (q)_{q∈S∖{p}}). The solutions therefore lie in the explicit finite box {x ∈ U_S : |v_p(x)| ≤ B for p ∈ S}, of 2(2B + 1)^{|S|} elements.

nodes.title: Product formula and height for S-units of a number field
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, S a finite set of finite places and y ∈ K^× with |y|_v = 1 for every finite place v ∉ S. Put ℓ_w(y) := m_w log w(y) for infinite places w and ℓ_v(y) := log|y|_v for v ∈ S. Then Σ_w ℓ_w(y) + Σ_{v∈S} ℓ_v(y) = 0 and logHeight₁(y) = Σ max(0, ℓ(y)) = ½Σ|ℓ(y)| over all places of S ∪ S_∞; in particular max|ℓ(y)| ≤ 2·logHeight₁(y).
hypotheses: Mathlib's normalisation: infinite places with multiplicity m_w, finite places normalised so that the product formula holds (NumberField.prod_abs_eq_one)
proofSteps: NumberField.prod_abs_eq_one: ∏_w w(y)^{m_w}·∏_v |y|_v = 1; factors at v ∉ S are 1; take logarithms.
NumberField.logHeight₁_eq: logHeight₁(y) = Σ_w m_w log⁺w(y) + Σ_v log⁺|y|_v; places outside S contribute 0.
Σ max(0, t) = ½Σ|t| when Σ t = 0.

nodes.title: Exponents in a finitely generated group are bounded by the height
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and γ₁, …, γ_t ∈ K^× multiplicatively independent (∏γ_j^{z_j} a root of unity only for z = 0). Let S be the finite set of finite places where some γ_j is not a unit and ℓ = (ℓ_v)_{v∈S∪S_∞} the S-logarithmic map. Then ℓ(γ₁), …, ℓ(γ_t) are ℝ-linearly independent, and with T_γ a left inverse of z ↦ Σz_jℓ(γ_j) and κ(γ) := 2‖T_γ‖: for every root of unity ζ ∈ K and z ∈ ℤ^t, max_j|z_j| ≤ κ(γ)·logHeight₁(ζ∏_jγ_j^{z_j}).
hypotheses: Multiplicative independence of the generators (every finitely generated Γ ⊂ K^× has such generators modulo its finite torsion)
proofSteps: ℓ is a homomorphism killing roots of unity, so ℓ(ζ∏γ^z) = Σz_jℓ(γ_j).
Discreteness: ‖ℓ(x)‖ ≤ 2 logHeight₁(x) (s-unit-log-height-identity) and NumberField.finite_setOfPred_logHeight₁_le (Northcott) show that bounded sets contain finitely many values ℓ(x).
Kernel: ℓ(x) = 0 forces logHeight₁(x) = 0, so x is a root of unity (NumberField.Embeddings.pow_eq_one_of_norm_eq_one applied to the integral element x); by independence z = 0.
A ℤ-basis of a discrete subgroup is ℝ-linearly independent (Real.finrank_eq_int_finrank_of_discrete).
|z_j| ≤ ‖T_γ‖‖ℓ(x)‖_∞ ≤ 2‖T_γ‖logHeight₁(x).
acceptance: Γ = (𝓞 K)^× with the fundamental units recovers unit-exponent-house-bound (S = ∅, logHeight₁ ≤ d log house).
K = ℚ, γ = (2, 3), S = {2, 3}: T_γ(ℓ) = (−ℓ₂/log 2, −ℓ₃/log 3) is a left inverse, κ = 2/log 2, and for x = 2/3 the bound reads 1 ≤ 2 log 3/log 2.

nodes.title: Explicit exponent bound for ax + by = 1 in a finitely generated group
nodes.statement: Let K, γ₁, …, γ_t, S, s and κ = κ(γ) be as in exponent-height-bound-for-finitely-generated-groups, a, b ∈ K^×, and C > 0 such that for every c ∈ {aζ, bζ : ζ root of unity in K} and every z ∈ ℤ^t with c∏γ_j^{z_j} ≠ 1: (i) |σ(c∏γ_j^{z_j}) − 1| ≥ (e·max(1, max|z_j|))^{−C} for every embedding σ : K →+* ℂ (Corollary 5.3), and (ii) |c∏γ_j^{z_j} − 1|_v ≥ (e·max(1, max|z_j|))^{−C} for every v ∈ S (Yu's theorem for algebraic numbers). Put M := max(house a, house b, max_{v∈S} max(|a|_v, |b|_v)), A := 2κs(log M + C), B₀ := 2κsC. Then every solution x = ζ_x∏γ_j^{z_j}, y = ζ_y∏γ_j^{w_j} of ax + by = 1 satisfies max_j max(|z_j|, |w_j|) ≤ max(1, 2A + 2B₀(log(2B₀) − 1)).
hypotheses: Hypothesis (ii) is the p-adic lower bound for linear forms in logarithms of algebraic numbers, a generalisation of Evertse's Theorem 5.16 (see gaps)
proofSteps: Assume B := max|w_j| ≥ max|z_j|, B ≥ 1 (else swap (x, a) and (y, b)); exponent-height-bound-for-finitely-generated-groups: B ≤ κ·logHeight₁(y).
small-place-of-s-unit: a place v with ℓ_v(y) ≤ −logHeight₁(y)/s ≤ −B/(κs).
v infinite: |σ_v(y)| ≤ e^{−B/(2κs)} (m_v ≤ 2), so |σ_v(ax) − 1| = |σ_v(by)| ≤ house(b)e^{−B/(2κs)}; v finite: |ax − 1|_v = |b|_v|y|_v ≤ |b|_v e^{−B/(κs)}.
Lower bound (i) or (ii) with c = aζ_x: (eB)^{−C} ≤ M e^{−B/(2κs)}.
Hence B ≤ 2κs(log M + C) + 2κsC·log B; log-linear-inequality-bound.

With K = ℚ, Γ = U_S only (ii) at the primes of S and (i) at ∞ are used; the S-unit equation over ℚ is recovered.

nodes.title: Divisors of m times S-units lie in finitely many cosets of a finitely generated group
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field with class number h, P a finite set of nonzero prime ideals of 𝓞 K, and for 𝔭 ∈ P let π_𝔭 ∈ 𝓞 K generate 𝔭^h. nodes.title: Effective finiteness of Thue–Mahler equations
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] be a binary form of degree d ≥ 3 with X^d-coefficient a₀ ≠ 0 such that F(X, 1) has at least three distinct complex zeros, m ≠ 0 an integer and p₁, …, p_s distinct primes. Then the set of (x, y, z₁, …, z_s) ∈ ℤ² × ℕ^s with gcd(x, y) = 1 and F(x, y) = m·p₁^{z₁}⋯p_s^{z_s} is finite, and its elements lie in an explicit region assembled from the bound of gyory-equation-exponent-bound (as in thue-equation-effective-bound).
hypotheses: gcd(x, y) = 1 is essential: otherwise (kx, ky) with k a product of the p_i gives infinitely many solutions
The reduction needs the Γ-unit equation (Theorem 5.18) over the splitting field, hence Yu's bound for algebraic numbers (DT.3)
proofSteps: thue-equation-monic-reduction with right-hand side a₀^{d−1}m∏p_i^{z_i}; gcd(a₀x, y) divides a₀, finitely many cases.
thue-form-factorisation: each x′ − θ_i y′ divides a₀^{d−1}m∏p_i^{z_i} in 𝓞 K, so v_𝔮(x′ − θ_i y′) ≤ v_𝔮(a₀^{d−1}m) for 𝔮 not above the p_i.
s-integral-divisor-representation with P = primes above p₁, …, p_s: x′ − θ_i y′ ∈ μ_iΓ_P with μ_i in a finite set.
siegel-identity gives a(μ)X + b(μ)Y = 1 with X, Y ∈ Γ_P; gyory-effective-finiteness leaves finitely many λ = (x′ − θ₀y′)/(x′ − θ₂y′), hence finitely many ξ = x′/y′ ∈ ℚ.
gcd(x, y) = 1 then leaves finitely many (x, y), and z is determined by F(x, y)/m; heights as in thue-equation-effective-bound.
acceptance: Tzanakis–de Weger (1992): x³ − 23x²y + 5xy² + 24y³ = ±2^{z₁}3^{z₂}5^{z₃}7^{z₄} has exactly 72 solutions with x > 0; ED.2's enumeration must reproduce them.
s = 0 is Theorem 5.13 (for coprime solutions).

nodes.title: D-finite (holonomic) power series
nodes.statement: Let k ⊆ ℂ be a subfield. A formal power series f ∈ ℂ[[z]] is D-finite over k if there are n ∈ ℕ and polynomials p₀, …, p_n ∈ k[z] with p_n ≠ 0 and Σ_{i=0}^{n} p_i(z)·f^{(i)} = 0, where f^{(i)} is the i-th formal derivative. Equivalently, the k(z)-span of f, f′, f″, … is finite-dimensional; equivalently (when the coefficients of f lie in k) the coefficient sequence is P-recursive: Σ_{i=0}^{r} q_i(n)·c_{n+i} = 0 for all n with q_i ∈ k[X], q_r ≠ 0.
hypotheses: k is a subfield of ℂ (in DT.5 always ℚ, Q̄ = algebraicClosure ℚ ℂ, or ℂ)
The equation is over k[z]; clearing denominators, this is the same as an equation over k(z)
proofSteps: Existential definition over polynomial coefficient tuples indexed by Fin (n + 1), with nonzero leading coefficient.

Closure under +, ×, derivative: the k(z)-spans of derivatives of f + g and fg lie in the span generated by products of derivatives, which is finite-dimensional (Beukers, AWS notes, proof of Proposition 3.2.1).
P-recursiveness: compare coefficients of z^m in Σ p_i f^{(i)} = 0.
acceptance: exp satisfies f′ − f = 0 over ℚ.
1/(1 − z) satisfies (1 − z)f′ − f = 0.
Σ z^{2^n} is not D-finite (it has the unit circle as natural boundary, while a D-finite series with finite radius has finitely many singularities).

nodes.title: The minimal differential equation of a D-finite series
nodes.statement: For a D-finite f over k, its minimal order ord_k(f) is the least n for which an equation Σ_{i=0}^{n} p_i f^{(i)} = 0 with p_i ∈ k[z], p_n ≠ 0 exists (dfiniteOrder). The minimal equations are unique up to a common rational factor: two minimal equations p, p′ satisfy p′_n p_i = p_n p′_i for all i; the monic minimal operator L = ∂^n + Σ_{i<n} (p_i/p_n) ∂^i is Beukers' 'minimal differential equation of f'. A point ξ ∈ ℂ is a singular point of L if the leading coefficient of every minimal equation vanishes at ξ (IsMinimalSingularPoint); a singular point ξ is apparent if L has a basis of solutions holomorphic at ξ.
hypotheses: The apparent-singularity notion uses the local solution space of L at ξ (holomorphic-solutions-of-linear-systems); it has no Lean statement until that API exists
Order 0 occurs only for f = 0
proofSteps: dfiniteOrder := Nat.find of the D-finiteness witness.
Uniqueness: if p, p′ are minimal, p′_n·(Σ p_i ∂^i) − p_n·(Σ p′_i ∂^i) annihilates f and has order < n, so all its coefficients vanish.
Singular points: a pole of some p_i/p_n; independent of the minimal equation chosen by uniqueness.
acceptance: exp: order 1, equation f′ − f = 0, no finite singular point.
(z − 1)eᶻ: order 1, minimal equation (z − 1)f′ = zf, singular (and apparent) at z = 1.
z: order 1 (z f′ − f = 0), singular at 0.

sources.locator: Section 1, after the definition of E-functions, p. 1
sources.excerpt: The linear differential equation Ly = 0 of minimal order which is satisfied by f is called the minimal differential equation of f.
sources.match: The definition; the singular points and apparent singularities are those of Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 2.2.

sources.excerpt: For example, the function (z−1)e^z is an E-function, and its minimal differential equation reads (z −1)f′ = zf. So we have a singularity at z = 1.
sources.match: The worked example used as a unit test.

nodes.title: E-functions
nodes.statement: A sequence a : ℕ → ℂ (the power series f(z) = Σ a_n zⁿ/n!) is an E-function if (i) every a_n is algebraic over ℚ; (ii) f is D-finite over Q̄; (iii) there is C > 0 with |σ(a_n)| ≤ C^{n+1} for every conjugate σ(a_n) (every root of the minimal polynomial of a_n); (iv) there are D > 0 and positive integers d_n ≤ D^{n+1} such that d_n a_m is an algebraic integer for all m ≤ n. The function eFun a : ℂ → ℂ, z ↦ Σ a_n zⁿ/n!, is entire. This is the geometric normalisation of Shidlovskii, André, Beukers and Fischler–Rivoal; Siegel's original definition allowed growth (n!)^ε and is not used.
hypotheses: The coefficients then lie in a single number field (the differential equation has finitely many algebraic coefficients)
Conventions: an E-function is recorded by its coefficient sequence a with the factorials divided out; the power series is ePowerSeries a
proofSteps: Structure with four fields as in the statement; ePowerSeries, eFun and the Hurwitz product hurwitzMul are auxiliary definitions.

Ring structure: (a + b) and the binomial convolution hurwitzMul a b satisfy (iii) with 2C and (iv) with D² (AWS Proposition 3.2.1, promoted to e-functions-form-a-ring); the shift a(n + 1) (derivative) satisfies the bounds with a larger constant.
Conjugates: applying a ring automorphism of ℂ to the coefficients preserves (i)–(iv) (conjugate differential equation, same minimal polynomials).
acceptance: exp (a_n = 1), J₀(−z²) and the hypergeometric series pF_q[a; b; z^{q−p+1}] with rational parameters are E-functions.
(z − 1)eᶻ has a_n = n − 1.

sources.excerpt: A power series F(z) = Σ an/n! z^n ∈ Q̄[[z]] is an E-function if (i) F(z) is solution of a non-zero linear differential equation with coefficients in Q̄(z). (ii) There exists C > 0 such that for any σ ∈ Gal(Q̄/Q) and any n ≥ 0, |σ(an)| ≤ C^{n+1}.
sources.match: Conditions (i)–(ii); (iii) is the denominator bound d_n ≤ D^{n+1}.

sources.excerpt: is called an E-function if 1. f(z) satisﬁes a linear diﬀerential equation with coeﬃcients in Q̄(z). 2. Both |an| and the common denominator den(a0, . . . , an) are bounded by an exponential bound of the form C^n, where C > 0 depends only on f.

nodes.title: G-functions
nodes.statement: A sequence a : ℕ → ℂ (the power series Σ a_n zⁿ) is a G-function if its coefficients are algebraic, Σ a_n zⁿ is D-finite over Q̄, all conjugates satisfy |σ(a_n)| ≤ C^{n+1}, and there are positive integers d_n ≤ D^{n+1} with d_n a_m integral for m ≤ n. Equivalently (Fischler–Rivoal), Σ a_n zⁿ is a G-function iff Σ a_n zⁿ/n! is an E-function. G-functions have a positive radius of convergence.
hypotheses: Same arithmetic conditions as E-functions, without the factorial
The equivalence with E-functions holds because a_n is P-recursive iff a_n/n! is

nodes.title: Mahler functions
nodes.statement: Let q ≥ 2 be an integer. A power series f ∈ ℂ[[z]] with algebraic coefficients is q-Mahler if there are polynomials p₀, …, p_n ∈ Q̄[z], not all zero, with p₀(z)f(z) + p₁(z)f(z^q) + ⋯ + p_n(z)f(z^{qⁿ}) = 0. Equivalently, f is a coordinate of a solution F = (f₁, …, f_m) of a Mahler system F(z) = A(z)F(z^q), A ∈ GL_m(Q̄(z)). The series f(z^r) is expandPow r f.
hypotheses: Coefficients algebraic (AF work with f ∈ Q̄{z}, convergent near 0)
q ≥ 2 is part of the data; the relation is over Q̄[z]
proofSteps: Existential definition as stated; expandPow r f has coefficient c_{m/r} at m when r ∣ m and 0 otherwise.
Ring structure: the Q̄(z)-span of {f(z^{q^i})} is finite-dimensional and stable under z ↦ z^q; products of two such spans are again finite-dimensional.
System form: take F = (f(z), f(z^q), …, f(z^{q^{n−1}})) and the companion matrix of the relation (after reducing to p₀p_n ≠ 0).
acceptance: Σ z^{2^n} is 2-Mahler: z f(z) − (1 + z) f(z²) + f(z⁴) = 0.
The Thue–Morse product ∏(1 − z^{2^n}) satisfies f(z) = (1 − z) f(z²).

sources.excerpt: Étant donné un entier q ≥ 2, une fonction f(z) ∈ Q̄{z} est dite q-mahlérienne s'il existe des polynômes p0(z), . . . , pn(z) ∈ Q̄[z], non tous nul, tels que (1.1) p0(z)f(z) + p1(z)f(z^q) + · · · + pn(z)f(z^{q^n}) = 0.

nodes.title: Regular points of a Mahler system
nodes.statement: Let q ≥ 2 and A ∈ GL_n(ℂ(z)) (a Mahler system F(z) = A(z)F(z^q)). A point α with 0 < |α| < 1 is regular if for no ℓ ≥ 0 is α^{q^ℓ} a pole of an entry of A or of A⁻¹ (with rational functions in lowest terms, poles are zeros of the denominator RatFunc.denom). Otherwise α is a singularity; the singularities have no accumulation point in the open unit disc.
hypotheses: ℓ ranges over all integers ≥ 0 (AF's 'entier positif' in the French sense)
A ∈ GL_n(Q̄(z)) in the applications
proofSteps: Definition by the displayed condition; the unfolding is isMahlerRegularPoint_iff.
α regular ⇒ α^q regular (shift ℓ).
Polynomial A with constant nonzero determinant: A and A⁻¹ have no poles, so every α with 0 < |α| < 1 is regular.
acceptance: For the Fredholm system (1, f) with A = [[1, 0], [z, 1]], every α is regular.
For A = (1 − 2z)⁻¹, α = 2^{−1/2} is singular although α is not a pole: α² = 1/2 is.

sources.excerpt: Un nombre complexe α du disque unité ouvert est une singularité du système (1.2) s'il existe un entier positif ℓ tel que α^{q^l} soit un pôle d'un coefficient d'une des matrices A(z) ou A(z)^{−1}.

nodes.title: Schanuel's conjecture (as an explicit hypothesis)
nodes.statement: SchanuelConjecture is the proposition: for every n and every z₁, …, z_n ∈ ℂ linearly independent over ℚ, the transcendence degree over ℚ of ℚ(z₁, …, z_n, e^{z₁}, …, e^{z_n}) is at least n. It is a statement, not an assumption of the library: every consequence in DT.5 takes it as a hypothesis.
hypotheses: ℚ-linear independence of the z_i (not algebraic independence)
The inequality is over ℚ; transcendence degree is Mathlib's Algebra.trdeg
proofSteps: Definition of the proposition with its complete body.
Unconditional instances: for algebraic z_i it is the Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem (DT.3), recorded as the API item schanuel_inequality_of_isAlgebraic; for n = 1 it is Hermite–Lindemann.
acceptance: The consequences algebraicIndependent_e_pi_of_schanuel and logarithmsConjecture_of_schanuel are proved from it.
No DT.5 theorem uses it unconditionally.

nodes.title: The conjecture on algebraic independence of logarithms (as an explicit hypothesis)
nodes.statement: LogarithmsAlgebraicIndependenceConjecture is the proposition: if ℓ₁, …, ℓ_n ∈ ℂ are logarithms of algebraic numbers (each e^{ℓ_i} algebraic) and are linearly independent over ℚ, then they are algebraically independent over ℚ.
hypotheses: Logarithms are any complex numbers with algebraic exponential (branches are part of the data)
proofSteps: Definition of the proposition.
Unconditional instances: n = 1 is Hermite–Lindemann; the linear shadow (linear independence over Q̄ of 1, ℓ₁, …, ℓ_n) is Baker's theorem (DT.3).
acceptance: Implied by Schanuel's conjecture (schanuel-implies-logarithms-conjecture).
It predicts log 2 and log 3 algebraically independent; open.
